zabid: Zabid was originally a village called al-Husayb, inhabited by the Asha'ir tribe, and it later took the name of the Wadi Zabid, the valley to its south. According to tradition, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, a companion of Muhammad, built the al-Asha'ir Mosque there as the fifth mosque in the history of Islam. The present town was created around 820 by Muhammad ibn Abdallah ibn Ziyad, whom the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun had sent to suppress a rebellion of the Asha'ir and Akk tribes. It was the capital of the Ziyadids until 1016, then of the Najahid dynasty and of the Mahdids until 1174.

Its mosques, among them the al-Asha'ir Mosque and the Great Mosque, became centres of Islamic learning, and its place on the road between Mecca and Aden brought prosperity. After the Ayyubids took Yemen in 1174, Zabid remained its economic and political centre. Under the Rasulids (1229–1454) the official capital moved to Taiz, but the rulers kept Zabid as a winter residence. The city then reached its height, with more palaces, gardens and religious institutions than any other in Yemen, and the 14th-century writer al-Khazraji claimed between 230 and 240 mosques. Ottoman authority arrived in 1539.

Zabid lies on Yemen's western coastal plain, in the Tihama region, with an urban population of around 52,590. Its historic quarter was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993, and the vestiges of its university can still be visited. In 2000 the site was placed on the List of World Heritage in Danger at the request of the Yemeni government because of poor upkeep: UNESCO reported that about 40% of the houses had been replaced by concrete buildings. The town grows indigo and cotton, and by the mid-20th century, in the account given in Muhammad Abdul-Wali's novel Sana'a: An Open City, it had become a backwater.
zadar: Zadar is the oldest continuously inhabited city in Croatia. It lies in northern Dalmatia on the Adriatic Sea, facing the islands of Ugljan and Pašman across the narrow Zadar Strait. The old city stands on a promontory that was once separated from the mainland by a deep moat, since filled in, and the harbour to the north-east is safe and spacious. Zadar was a Liburnian settlement laid out in the 9th century BCE and called Iader. By the 7th century BCE it was an important centre of trade with the Phoenicians, Etruscans and Greeks, and it became the main seat of the Liburnian sea power.

It became a Roman municipium in 59 BCE and a colony in 48 BCE, with a regular street grid, a forum and a capitolium. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 CE it became the capital of the Byzantine Theme of Dalmatia. It was briefly under Frankish rule at the start of the 9th century, and in 998 it sought the protection of Venice against Neretvian pirates and swore allegiance to Doge Pietro II Orseolo. Control passed repeatedly between Venice and the Kingdom of Hungary. In 1202 the Venetians, with the Crusaders, reconquered and plundered the city, and in 1358 the Treaty of Zadar gave it to Hungary.

On 31 July 1409 Ladislaus of Naples sold Zadar and his dynasty's rights to Dalmatia to Venice for 100,000 ducats. It became the de facto capital of Venetian Dalmatia and, once the Ottoman Empire had conquered the hinterland, a stronghold protecting Venetian trade. Between the 15th and 17th centuries it was an important Renaissance centre, producing the sculptor Giorgio da Sebenico and Giovanni Francesco Fortunio, who wrote the first Italian grammar, and Croatian writers such as Petar Zoranić and Šime Budinić.

After the Treaty of Campo Formio in 1797 it passed to Austria, and from 1815 to 1918 it was capital of the Kingdom of Dalmatia. In the 19th century it was a centre of the Illyrian movement, amid growing polarisation between Croats and Dalmatian Italians, who then formed a majority of its citizens. Italy took it after the First World War, and the Partisans captured it on 1 November 1944. In 1947 it became part of the Socialist Republic of Croatia. About 10,000 Italians left, and the last Italian schools closed in 1953.

Zadar is the seat of Zadar County and the northern Dalmatian region, and the fifth-largest city in Croatia. The University of Zadar traces its origin to a Dominican institution of 1396, which closed in 1807 and was re-established in 1956. The Roman forum, parts of the aqueduct and the medieval churches survive, and UNESCO included its fortifications in the Venetian Works of Defence in 2017.
zagan: Żagań lies on the Bóbr river in western Poland, in the historic region of Lower Silesia, roughly halfway between Cottbus and Wrocław. The Bóbr and the Kwisa meet just outside the town. The name probably means place of the burnt forest, from the burning of primeval forest by early settlers, which fits the names of nearby places such as Żary, Zgorzelec and Pożarów. It is known in German and French as Sagan.

The area belonged to Poland after the creation of the state in the 10th century. Żagań was founded in the 12th century by Bolesław IV the Curly and first mentioned in a deed of 1202, when it belonged to the Duchy of Silesia. It received town rights between 1248 and 1260. After the death of Duke Konrad I of Głogów in 1274, his youngest son Przemko became Duke of Żagań in 1278 and founded a monastery of Augustinian Canons. The duchy was divided and reunited several times among Piast heirs, and from 1329 its dukes were vassals of John of Luxembourg, King of Bohemia.

Piast rule ended when Jan II the Mad sold the duchy to Duke Albert III of Saxony of the House of Wettin. In 1549 Elector Maurice of Saxony ceded it to Ferdinand I of Habsburg, and in 1627 Emperor Ferdinand II gave the fief to Albrecht von Wallenstein. It then passed to the Bohemian Lobkowicz family. After the First Silesian War of 1742 Żagań became part of Prussia. In 1786 Peter von Biron, Duke of Courland, bought the fief, and in 1845 his daughter Dorothea was invested as Duchess of Sagan.

Żagań has 23,136 inhabitants and is the capital of Żagań County in the Lubusz Voivodeship. Its main sights are the former Augustinian monastery, a burial site of the Piast dynasty, the Ducal Palace and Park ensemble, and the POW Camps Museum. The museum stands on the site of German prisoner-of-war camps that held over 60,000 Allied soldiers, among them Stalag Luft III, the scene of the Great Escape, an episode filmed in 1963.
zagreb: Zagreb lies in the north of Croatia, along the Sava River, on the southern slopes of the Medvednica mountain and near the border with Slovenia, at an elevation of about 158 metres. Most of its districts lie low in the Sava valley, while the northern and northeastern ones spread across the foothills of Medvednica. Its position, where Central Europe, the Mediterranean and Southeast Europe meet, has made it the centre of Croatia's road, rail and air networks.

The oldest known settlement near present-day Zagreb was the Roman town of Andautonia, now Šćitarjevo, which existed between the first and fifth centuries CE. The city's own history begins in 1094, when the Hungarian King Ladislaus, returning from a campaign against the Kingdom of Croatia, founded a diocese. Beside the bishop's see grew the canonical settlement of Kaptol, north of Zagreb Cathedral, and on the neighbouring hill the fortified settlement of Gradec. The name Zagreb is first recorded in a charter by Felician, Archbishop of Esztergom.

Both settlements were attacked by the Mongols in 1242. Béla IV, king of Croatia and Hungary, had been given a safe haven in Gradec, and in gratitude granted it the Golden Bull of 1242, which exempted its citizens from county rule and gave them autonomy and their own judicial system. The name is probably from a Proto-Slavic word meaning a hill or an embankment, perhaps the remains of first-millennium fortifications on Grič.

In the mid-19th century the Ban of Croatia, Josip Jelačić, united Gradec and Kaptol, and the main city square bears his name. The University of Zagreb was founded in 1669. While Croatia was part of Yugoslavia, from 1918 to 1991, Zagreb was an important economic centre and the second largest city. After Croatia declared independence in 1991 its Parliament proclaimed Zagreb the capital.

Zagreb is the capital and largest city of Croatia and the seat of its government, parliament and Constitutional Court, which stand on St. Mark's Square. It has the special status of a city and a county, separate from Zagreb County. The University of Zagreb is the oldest continuously operating university in Croatia.
zagros-mountains: The Zagros range is 1,600 km long and spans Iran, northern Iraq and south-eastern Turkey. It begins in north-western Iran, follows Iran's western border, and runs south-east to end at the Strait of Hormuz. Its highest point is Mount Dena, at 4,409 metres. The mountains were formed mainly by the collision of the Eurasian and Arabian plates, chiefly during the Miocene, and the collision continues. They are entirely of sedimentary origin, made mainly of limestone, and are divided into many parallel sub-ranges. Salt domes are common, and Iran's main oilfields lie in the western central foothills.

Humans have lived in the Zagros since the Lower Paleolithic. The earliest human fossils found there are Neanderthal, from Shanidar Cave, Bisitun Cave and Wezmeh Cave, with the remains of ten Neanderthals at Shanidar dating from about 65,000 to 35,000 years ago. Signs of early agriculture in the foothills go back as far as 9000 BCE, and some settlements later grew into cities such as Anshan and Susa. Wine storage from between 3500 and 5400 BCE has been found at Hajji Firuz Tepe and Godin Tepe, among the earliest evidence of wine production.

In ancient times the Zagros was the home of peoples such as the Hurrians, Guti, Kassites, Elamites, Turukku and Lullubi, who periodically invaded the Sumerian, Akkadian and Assyrian cities of Mesopotamia. The mountains form a geographic barrier between the Mesopotamian plain and the Iranian plateau. A small archive of clay tablets from Tell Shemshara on the Little Zab records the interactions of these groups in the early second millennium BCE. Ancient Mesopotamians placed the entrance to the underworld in the Zagros, with a staircase leading down to its gates.

The Zagros has long been home to pastoralists and farmers, among them Lurs, Bakhtiari, Kurds and Qashqai, who move their herds from the eastern slopes in summer to the western slopes in winter. Cities at the foothills include Sulaymaniyah, Kermanshah, Khorramabad and Shiraz. Oak woodland and pistachio and almond steppe remain, though overgrazing and deforestation have degraded them, and the ancestors of wheat, barley, lentil, almond, pistachio, pomegranate and grape grow wild there.
zaire: Zaire was the Congolese state in Central Africa that Mobutu Sese Seko headed from 1965 to 1997. In 1965 the division of power between president and parliament in Congo-Léopoldville, a former Belgian colony, led to a stalemate, as it had in 1960. Joseph-Désiré Mobutu again seized power, but this time he took the presidency himself, following five years of upheaval after independence known as the Congo Crisis. The country was officially the Democratic Republic of the Congo until 1971. On 27 October 1971 he announced its renaming as the Republic of Zaire.

The name derives from the Congo River, sometimes called Zaire in Portuguese, which in turn comes from the Kikongo nzere o zadi, the river that swallows rivers. Under the policy of authenticité Zairians were required to adopt African names, and Mobutu himself became Mobutu Sese Seko. Cities were renamed too, so that Léopoldville became Kinshasa and Stanleyville became Kisangani.

By 1967 Mobutu had given the country a new constitution, approved by 98 per cent of those voting in a referendum in June, which centralised executive power in the president. On 17 April 1967 he created the Popular Movement of the Revolution, the MPR, as the only party. In the presidential election of 1 November 1970 only the MPR could nominate a candidate, and Mobutu was confirmed with 10,131,000 votes against 157.

They were driven out with Western military help. By 1979 purchasing power was only 4 per cent of its level in 1960, and IMF loans from 1976 were largely embezzled. After the end of the Cold War Mobutu had to declare a new republic in 1990 and allow a multi-party system. In 1996 Hutu militias that had fled Rwanda, allied with the Zairian army, attacked Congolese Tutsis in the east, and the Tutsi militias rose in the First Congo War. Laurent-Désiré Kabila led the rebellion, Mobutu fled, and the name Democratic Republic of the Congo was restored in 1997. Mobutu died less than four months later in Morocco.

Zaire was a unitary presidential state in which the president appointed and dismissed ministers, provincial governors and judges. Its doctrine, Mobutism, was set out in the Manifesto of N'sele of May 1967, which named nationalism, revolution and authenticity as its themes and declared the regime neither right nor left. Authenticity also led Zairians to abandon Western dress for the abacost. The currency was the zaïre, divided into 100 makuta.
zakat: The word zakat comes from the Arabic root z-k-w, meaning to purify. Muslims hold that it purifies income and wealth, as ablutions purify the body and prayer the soul. The Quran discusses charity in many verses, and zakat is found in the early Medinan suras and described as obligatory. Muslims believe that those who give it can expect reward from God in the afterlife. The practice is traditionally traced to Muhammad, and Schact suggested that the idea may have entered Islam from Judaism, from the Hebrew and Aramaic word zakut, though some Islamic scholars disagree.

The caliph Abu Bakr was the first to institute a statutory zakat system, on the principle that it must be paid to the legitimate representative of Muhammad's authority. Tribes that refused to pay while remaining nominally Muslim were considered apostates, which led to the Ridda wars. Uthman ibn Affan decreed that only apparent wealth was taxable, which limited zakat mostly to agricultural land and produce. After Ali ibn Abu Talib his supporters refused to pay it to Muawiyah I.

State administration in Medina was short-lived. During the reign of Umar bin Abdul Aziz (717–720 CE) it is reported that no one in Medina needed zakat, and after him it came to be seen more as an individual responsibility. Zakat was not collected from non-Muslims, who paid the jizya, and Muslims were also encouraged to give voluntary sadaqat.

Zakat on wealth is customarily 2.5 per cent, or one fortieth, of disposable income after essential needs. It is payable on assets held for a lunar year above the nisab, a minimum value, and on agricultural goods, precious metals, minerals and livestock the rate varies between 2.5 and 20 per cent. Scholars differ on the nisab and on which kinds of wealth are zakatable.

Verse 9:60 of the Quran is read as naming eight categories of recipient: the poor, the needy, the collectors, those whose hearts are to be won, those to be freed from slavery, debtors, those in the cause of God, and stranded travellers. The Shafi'i school requires equal division among the categories, while the Hanafi school permits giving to any or only one. Shia Muslims have traditionally given zakat to deputies of the imams rather than to the state.
zakopane: Zakopane lies in a valley between the Tatra Mountains and Gubałówka Hill, 800 to 1,100 metres above sea level, near Poland's border with Slovakia. It centres on the crossing of Krupówki and Kościuszko Streets and is connected by rail and road to Kraków. Its altitude makes it almost 3 °C colder than Kraków, and its position on the northern slope of the Tatras brings far more precipitation than the lowlands to the north. A warm foehn wind, known locally as halny, can sharply raise winter temperatures. The town is a centre of Goral culture and is often called the winter capital of Poland.

The earliest documents mentioning Zakopane date from the 17th century and describe a glade called Zakopisko. In 1676 it was a village of 43 inhabitants, and in 1818 it had 1,805 inhabitants. The first church was built in 1847. In the 19th century it became a centre of mining and metallurgy, the largest in Galicia, and by 1889 it had grown into a climatic health resort. Rail services began on 1 October 1899, and by the end of the 1800s the population was about 3,000.

The ski jump on Wielka Krokiew opened in 1925, the cable car to Kasprowy Wierch was finished in 1936 and the funicular to Gubałówka in 1938. By 1930 there were about 60,000 tourists a year. Germany invaded in September 1939, and the Germans set up a prison camp for Poles in the town. The Polish resistance attacked a German prison on 29 November 1939 and used Zakopane as an underground staging point between Poland and Hungary. In 1944 the Germans deported thousands of people from Warsaw to the town after the Warsaw Uprising, and the occupation ended in January 1945.

The Zakopane Style of architecture, inspired by the regional art of Podhale, was pioneered by Stanisław Witkiewicz, and its main examples include Villa Koliba of 1892–93, Villa Oksza of 1894–95 and the Chapel in Jaszczurówka of 1904–07. Many artists lived or worked in the town during the Young Poland period, among them the composer Karol Szymanowski, whose Villa Atma is now a museum. The Old Cemetery in Pęksowy Brzyzek holds the graves of many artists and mountaineers. Zakopane hosted the Nordic World Ski Championships in 1929, 1939 and 1962. It is part of Lesser Poland Voivodeship.
zakynthos: Zakynthos lies in the eastern Ionian Sea about 20 kilometres west of the Peloponnese, with Kefalonia 15 kilometres to the north. It is about 40 kilometres long and 20 wide, covers 405.55 square kilometres and has an arrowhead shape, with Cape Skinari at its north-western tip. The west is a mountainous plateau with steep cliffs, while the east is a fertile plain with long sandy beaches, overlooked by the hill of Bochali. Its highest point is Vrachionas, at 758 metres. The town of Zakynthos, also called Chora, is the capital.

Homer mentions the island in the Iliad and the Odyssey, and tradition names its first settler as Zakynthos, son of the Arcadian king Dardanos. During the First Peloponnesian War the Athenian commander Tolmides made an alliance with the island. It gave Athens a source of tar, dredged from a lake now called Lake Keri, which protected the planking of the Athenian triremes. In 430 BCE a Spartan force under the admiral Cnemus burned much of the countryside but failed to take the city. Rome finally conquered the island in 191 BCE under Marcus Fulvius Nobilior.

In 459 the Vandals under Geiseric plundered the island and carried off 500 aristocrats. After Margaritus of Brindisi captured it in 1185 it formed part of the County Palatine of Cephalonia and Zakynthos, and a Latin bishopric stood beside the Orthodox one. Venetian rule lasted until the fall of the Republic of Venice in 1797. The island then passed through French rule, the Septinsular Republic from 1800, French rule again in 1807 and British control from 1809, until the Union of the Ionian Islands with Greece in 1864.

Under Venice, Zakynthos had closer contact with western literary trends than other areas inhabited by Greek people, and in the late 18th century it produced the Heptanese School of poetry. Its best-known poet is Dionysios Solomos, whose statue stands in the main town square. During the Axis occupation in the Second World War, the mayor Loukas Karrer and Bishop Chrysostomos Dimitriou refused to hand over a list of the town's Jewish community and hid its members in rural villages. According to some sources all 275 Jews of the island survived, and both men were recognised as Righteous among the Nations.
zambezi: The river is 2,574 km long and drains a basin of 1,390,000 km2, slightly less than half the size of the Nile's. It rises in a marshy dambo in miombo woodland in North-Western Province, Zambia, and flows south-west into Angola for about 240 km before turning south. It then runs along the north-eastern border of Namibia and the northern border of Botswana, follows the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe, and crosses Mozambique to the Indian Ocean.

The upper river falls about 400 m between its source and the Chavuma Falls, then only another 180 m across some 800 km to Victoria Falls, which mark the boundary with the middle river. Below the falls the river runs for about 200 km through the Batoka Gorge, between basalt walls 20 to 60 m apart. The lower river, 650 km from Cahora Bassa to the sea, is navigable but shallow in the dry season.

Vasco da Gama anchored in January 1498 at what he called the Rio dos Bons Sinais, now the Quelimane, which was then linked to the Zambezi by navigable channels. By the 16th century the river was called the Cuama, after a Swahili coast outpost in its delta. Medieval geographers knew the region as the Empire of Monomotapa, and early maps probably drew on Arab information. The Portuguese degredado António Fernandes visited the inland river in 1511 and 1513 to report on trade; his findings showed the importance of the upper Zambezi ports to the East African gold trade.

The rapids prevented the river from becoming a long-distance route. David Livingstone's Zambezi expedition tried to open it to paddle steamers but was defeated by the Cahora Bassa rapids. A paddle-barge service later ran between the Katombora Rapids and the rapids above Katima Mulilo, with Lozi paddlers and teams of oxen hauling barges round the Ngonye Falls.

Lake Kariba, created in 1959 behind the Kariba Dam, is one of the largest man-made lakes in the world, and the Cahora Bassa Dam in Mozambique was completed in 1973. Together the dams control the seasonal floods, and the delta is now about half as broad as before. Filling Cahora Bassa in a single flood season cut mangrove cover by 40 per cent and the prawn catch by 60 per cent.
zambia: Zambia covers 752,614 square kilometres and consists mostly of high plateaus with some hills and mountains, dissected by river valleys. About three-quarters of the country drains to the Zambezi and Kafue basin and about a quarter to the Congo basin. The Zambezi flows through the west and forms the southern border with Namibia, Botswana and Zimbabwe, and two of its largest tributaries, the Kafue and the Luangwa, flow mainly in Zambia. In the east the plateau rises from about 900 metres in the south to 1,800 metres in the north near Mbala. The highest point is Mafinga Central, at 2,339 metres, in the Mafinga Hills.

The fossil skull of Broken Hill Man, also called Kabwe Man, dated between 300,000 and 125,000 years ago, shows that early humans lived in the area. Zambia was inhabited by the Khoisan and Batwa peoples until around 300 CE, when migrating Bantu began to settle. Rock art such as the Mwela Rock Paintings, the Mumbwa Caves and Nachikufu Cave is attributed to these early hunter-gatherers.

The Bantu originally lived around present-day Cameroon and Nigeria and about 5,000 years ago began a millennia-long expansion across much of the continent, one of the largest human migrations in history, and are believed to have been the first to bring iron working into large parts of Africa. The first Bantu communities in Zambia lived in villages without an organised unit under a chief, moved as slash-and-burn farming exhausted the soil, kept cattle, and were highly self-sufficient.

After European expeditions in the eighteenth century, the British Empire began to consolidate control following the 1890 British Ultimatum against the Portuguese. Britain formed the protectorates of Barotziland–North-Western Rhodesia and North-Eastern Rhodesia, merged in 1911 as Northern Rhodesia. For most of the colonial period an administration appointed from London governed the territory with the advice of the British South Africa Company. Industrial copper mining began on the Copperbelt in the late 1920s and triggered rapid urbanisation. Zambia became independent on 24 October 1964 with Kenneth Kaunda as the first president, and from 1972 to 1991 it was a one-party state.

Lusaka is the capital, in the south-central part of the country, and the population is concentrated around it and in the Copperbelt Province. The name Zambia derives from the Zambezi river, and the territory was called Northern Rhodesia from 1911 to 1964. The country nominally includes about 73 ethnic groups, most of them Bantu-speaking, of which the Bemba, Nyanja and Tonga are the largest. The Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa has its headquarters in Lusaka.
zamboanga-city: The southwest and eastern sides of the city are bounded by irregular, generally rocky coastlines with occasional sandy or gravelly beaches, and the coast usually descends abruptly towards the sea. The terrain ranges from rolling to very steep, with a highest elevation of 1,200 metres. The city has mangrove areas at Tagasilay and eastern Vitali Island, and the Pasonanca Watershed Forest Reserve. The name is the Hispanicized spelling of the Sinama samboangan, meaning mooring place, from samboang, a mooring pole.

The Zamboanga Peninsula was settled in the late 12th or early 13th century by the Subanen people, and it was also the homeland of the ancestors of the Yakan, the Balanguingui and other closely related Sama-Bajau peoples. Spanish explorers led by Ferdinand Magellan reached the Philippine archipelago in 1521, and in 1569 Zamboanga was chosen as the site of a Spanish settlement and garrison at La Caldera, now part of Barangay Recodo. Spain gave the former local polity protectorate status against the Sulu Sultanate, its former overlord. The city became one of the main Spanish strongholds in Mindanao, supporting colonial efforts in the south, paving the way for Christian settlements and serving as an outpost against foreign invaders and Moro pirates.

The Republic of Zamboanga was proclaimed on 28 May 1899, after Zamboangueño revolutionary forces defeated the last Spanish government there. Fort Pilar was turned over to General Vicente Álvarez, who was its first president until November 1899. The republic lasted until 1903, with Isidoro Midel as second president under a puppet government of the United States, followed by Mariano Arquiza. After its dissolution Zamboanga became the capital of the Moro Province, a semi-military government of five districts, and General John J. Pershing was its military governor from 1909 to 1914.

Zamboanga became a chartered city on 12 October 1936 under Commonwealth Act No. 39, with a territory that included the whole island of Basilan. Japanese forces landed there on 2 March 1942, and the city became a branch hub of Unit 731, where Japanese doctors carried out human experimentation on Filipinos. Basilan was made a separate city on 16 July 1948.

The 2024 census counted 1,018,894 people. Roman Catholicism is the predominant religion, with 56.93% of the population, followed by Islam and Evangelical Protestantism. The lingua franca is Chavacano, whose lexifier is Spanish and whose grammar is influenced by Subanon and other Austronesian languages of the Philippines; Tausug is the second most spoken language. Sardine canning is concentrated on the west coast, and the traditional sailboat, the vinta, is known around Zamboanga for its colourful sails.
zamboanga-del-norte: Zamboanga del Norte lies in the Zamboanga Peninsula region of Mindanao and covers 7,301 square kilometres in the northern part of the peninsula. It borders Zamboanga del Sur and Zamboanga Sibugay to the south, Misamis Occidental to the northeast and the Sulu Sea to the north and west. Its irregular coastline runs some 400 kilometres from north to south. The average elevation is 243.8 metres, the highest peak being Mount Dabiak in Katipunan at 2,600 metres, and the land near the coast is plain. Rainfall is evenly distributed through the year, giving a mild climate.

The name Zamboanga is the Hispanicized form of the Sinama term samboangan, "mooring place", from samboang, "mooring pole"; it is attested in historical records from the 17th century. Islam was the predominant religion until the Spanish spread Christianity through the Jesuits, Augustinians and Dominicans. The Jesuit missionary Francesco Palliola of Nola was active in Dapitan and died at Ponot, now the town of Jose Dalman.

Before its creation as a province, the area formed the northern portion of the historical province of Zamboanga. Republic Act No. 711, issued on 6 June 1952, divided Zamboanga into two provinces, one of them Zamboanga del Sur. During the martial law that began in September 1972, the human rights lawyers Jacobo Amatong and Zorro Aguilar were shot dead by two soldiers who were never caught, and the acupuncturist Leo Alto, who helped Subanon communities defend their ancestral lands, was killed by the Philippine Constabulary at Polanco on 1 August 1975.

The capital and largest city is Dipolog. The province has 25 municipalities and 2 cities, and the 2020 census counted 1,047,455 people. Cebuano is the main language, with Chavacano, Subanon, Tausug, Samal, Filipino and English also spoken, and about half the people are Roman Catholic. Dapitan is the town where the national hero José Rizal was exiled by the Spanish colonial authorities. About half the land is farmed, mainly for corn, coconut and rice, and yellow fin tuna is the main catch of the commercial fishery.
zamfara-state: Zamfara State lies in the North-West geopolitical zone of Nigeria. It is bordered by Sokoto to the north-west and west, Kebbi to the south-west, Niger and Kaduna to the south and Katsina to the east, and a short stretch of its northern border forms part of the international border with the Niger. It takes its name from the Zamfara River, which flows through it, and from the historic Kingdom of Zamfara. The state lies almost entirely within the West Sudanian savanna and contains the Ka, Rima, Sokoto and Zamfara rivers. Its population is mainly Hausa and Fulani, and the great majority are Muslim.

The Kingdom of Zamfara was one of the old Hausa kingdoms, like Kano, Katsina, Gobir, Kebbi and Zazzau. It was established in the 11th century and flourished as a city-state until the 16th century, and its capital moved between places such as Dutsi and Birnin Zamfara. In the 16th century it became a tributary of the Kebbi Kingdom under Kanta Kotal, and it regained its independence by a revolt around 1715. Gobir destroyed Birnin Zamfara in the first half of the 18th century, and the court eventually moved to Anka. Zamfara was incorporated into the Sokoto Caliphate in the Fulani jihad of 1804 led by Usman dan Fodio.

After the British conquered the Caliphate in 1903 the area became part of the Northern Nigeria Protectorate, and Nigeria became independent in 1960. It formed part of the Northern Region until 1967, then of the North-Western State, and from 1976 of Sokoto State. On 1 October 1996 the military government of Sani Abacha separated the eastern local government areas as Zamfara State, with an area of 38,418 square kilometres. Its first governor was Jibril Yakubu.

Gusau is the state capital and largest city. It grew under British rule into a commercial and administrative centre on the road and rail network. The state has fourteen local government areas, and more than 80 per cent of its people are engaged in agriculture, growing millet, guinea corn, maize, rice, groundnuts and cotton and herding livestock. Its slogan is Farming is Our Pride. Zamfara was the first Nigerian state to adopt Sharia criminal law.
zapatista-army-of-national-liberation: Chiapas had seen earlier uprisings, among them the Caste War or Chamula Rebellion of 1867–1870 and the Pajarito War of 1911. The EZLN emerged under the Institutional Revolutionary Party, which had ruled Mexico for more than sixty years, and many young people considered legal channels of political participation closed. The National Liberation Forces, founded in Monterrey on 6 August 1969, were one of the clandestine groups that sought to overthrow the regime. The EZLN was founded on 17 November 1983 by non-indigenous members of those forces from the urban north and by indigenous inhabitants of the Las Cañadas and Lacandon Jungle regions of eastern Chiapas.

The group grew slowly, building on peasant organisations and the Catholic Church. Through the efforts of the Diocese of San Cristóbal de Las Casas, most indigenous communities in the Lacandon forest were already politically active in the 1970s. In 1992 an amendment of Article 27 of the Constitution ended land reform, which increased unrest among indigenous peasants.

The EZLN went public on 1 January 1994, issuing its First Declaration and Revolutionary Laws from the Lacandon Jungle, which amounted to a declaration of war on a government it considered illegitimate. About 3,000 armed insurgents seized six towns and cities in the Chiapas highlands and soon retreated to the forest to avoid a federal offensive. Its demands included work, land, housing, food, healthcare, education, independence, liberty, democracy, justice and peace. After a ceasefire on 12 January, peace talks began with the Catholic bishop Samuel Ruiz acting for the Zapatistas and Manuel Camacho Solis for the state.

In 1995 the army besieged the group in the Lacandon Jungle, but President Zedillo abandoned the offensive for a diplomatic approach. After the election of Vicente Fox in 2001 the army withdrew from some positions, but the EZLN rejected the resulting agreement and created 32 autonomous municipalities. In 2005 it issued the Sixth Declaration of the Lacandon Jungle, extending its cause to all the exploited and dispossessed of Mexico.

The Zapatistas describe themselves as a decentralised organisation. Political decisions are deliberated in community assemblies, while military and organisational matters are decided by the General Command, a committee of area elders. Its ideology, called Neozapatismo, combines Maya tradition with elements of Catholic liberation theology and indigenous autonomism, and it has avoided adherence to a specific political ideology beyond the left. One Zapatista slogan is Para todos todo, para nosotros nada, meaning everything for everyone, nothing for us.
zaporozhian-cossacks: The name comes from Zaporizhzhia, "the land beyond the rapids", where the fortress of the Zaporozhians, the Sich, stood. Cossack is traced to a Turkic word meaning a free man, and the Cossacks were predominantly Ruthenians who included other groups. It is not clear when the first Cossack communities formed on the Lower Dnieper; similar people lived on the steppe from the 12th century, and the part played by nomads such as the Cumans, Pechenegs and Khazars in their origins is disputed. Many were escaped serfs who preferred the dangerous freedom of the steppe to life under Polish or Polonised aristocrats, and newcomers had to accept Eastern Orthodoxy. In the 16th century Dmytro Vyshnevetsky, a Ruthenian noble, united these groups into a strong military organization.

In the 16th century the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth regarded the Zaporozhians as its subjects, though tentatively, and registered Cossacks were part of its army until 1699. From the later 16th century their raids on Ottoman territory, which Tatar raids answered, strained relations between the Commonwealth and the Ottoman Empire and helped lead to wars such as the Battle of Cecora in 1620. After the Treaty of Pereyaslav in 1654 the Host became a suzerainty under the protection of the tsar of Russia, though it long kept near-complete autonomy.

By the late 18th century much of the Cossack officer class in Ukraine had been absorbed into the Russian nobility, and many rank-and-file Cossacks had been reduced to peasant status. The Sich sheltered runaway serfs, which angered Catherine II. Her council decided on 7 May 1775 to disband it. General Peter Tekeli surrounded the Sich with artillery and infantry on 5 June, and the Cossacks were overwhelmed. In 1784 Grigory Potemkin formed the Host of the Loyal Zaporozhians between the Southern Bug and the Dniester.

The Host was governed by the unwritten Cossack Code. It had 38 kurins and five to eight palankas, and all officers were elected by the General Military Council for a year on 1 January. Its leader never officially held the title of hetman, though Cossack leaders were unofficially called so. The highest body was the Sich Rada, the council that decided matters of foreign and internal policy, elections, the division of land and the punishment of grave crimes, which is why some sources call the Sich a Cossack republic. Hetmans and kish otamans carried the bulawa, or mace; the one carried by Bohdan Khmelnytsky from 1648 was silver, covered in gold and set with pearls and gems.
zaragoza: Zaragoza lies on the Ebro river and its tributaries, the Huerva and the Gállego, roughly in the centre of both Aragon and the Ebro basin. It stands at about 208 metres above sea level in a rather arid depression, with a semi-arid climate and a cold, dry northwest wind in winter called the Cierzo. The site lies near the middle of the hexagon formed by Bilbao, Madrid, Valencia, Barcelona, Bordeaux and Toulouse.

A village of the Sedetani, an Iberian tribe, called Salduie stood here first. Augustus founded the city as Caesaraugusta between 25 and 11 BCE as a colony for army veterans of the Cantabrian wars. It had a forum, baths and a theatre, and the Goths took it in the fifth century CE without significant bloodshed or destruction. After the Umayyad conquest of the eighth century it became capital of the Upper March of al-Andalus, with the name Saraqusta.

In 1018, amid the collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba, it became an independent taifa, first under the Tujibid family and from 1039 under the Banu Hud, whose rulers included Ahmad al-Muqtadir and Yusuf al-Mu'taman ibn Hud. The taifa flourished in the late 11th century. It fell to the Almoravids in 1110 and was conquered in 1118, after which it became the political and spiritual centre of the Kingdom of Aragon. Bubonic plague in 1564 reportedly killed about 10,000 of an estimated population of 25-30,000.

During the Peninsular War the city withstood two sieges by the Napoleonic army, from June to August 1808 and from December 1808 to February 1809, and surrendered only after some 50,000 defenders had died.

Zaragoza is the capital of the autonomous community of Aragon, with a population of 699,007. The Basílica del Pilar, La Seo Cathedral, built over the city's main mosque, and the Aljafería Palace are its best-known buildings, and several of them belong to the Mudéjar Architecture of Aragon, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Fiestas del Pilar last nine days, with their main day on 12 October.
zaranj: Zaranj lies in the western part of Nimruz Province in southwestern Afghanistan, near the Iranian border, at about 476 metres above sea level. Its water comes from the Khash and Helmand rivers. The climate is hot desert, with very hot summers when temperatures may approach 50 °C, cool winters and very little rain. The city stands on an important trade route linking Central Asia, East Asia and South Asia with the Middle East, and the Pul-i-Abresham border crossing lies in its west.

Zaranj bears the name of an ancient city, attested in Old Persian as Zranka and in Middle Persian as Zrang, which in Greek became Drangiana. The word derives from the Old Persian zaranka, "waterland". The Achaemenid Zranka, capital of Drangiana, was almost certainly at Dahan-e Gholaman, southeast of Zabol in Iran. After that city was abandoned its name passed to later administrative centres of the region, which came to be known as Sakastan, then Sijistan and finally Sistan. Medieval Zaranj stood at Nad-i Ali, 4.4 km north of the modern city. According to Arab geographers, it was founded by people who left Ram Shahristan, the earlier capital of Sistan, after its dam on the Helmand canal broke.

Zaranj surrendered to the governor of Khurasan in 652 and became a base for further caliphal expansion. A Nestorian Christian community is recorded there in the sixth century, and a Jacobite diocese by the end of the eighth. In the 9th century it was the capital of the Saffarid dynasty, founded by Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar, a local coppersmith turned warlord. Defeated by the Samanids in 900, the Saffarids were conquered by Mahmud of Ghazni in 1003. Zaranj later served as the capital of the Nasrid (1029-1225) and Mihrabanid (1236-1537) maliks of Nimruz. In 1738 Nader Shah of Khorasan removed the Hotak dynasty, who had captured it in the early 18th century.

Zaranj is the capital of Nimruz Province, which was separated from Farah-Chakansur Province in 1968 to form Nimruz and Farah. Nimruz University is the largest of its universities. Ethnic groups were reported in 2007 as Baloch 44%, Pashtun 34% and Tajik 22%.
zaria: The old part of Zaria, known as Birnin Zazzau or Zaria City, was originally surrounded by walls and a fortress, most of which have been removed. The Emir's palace stands in the old city. In the old city and the adjacent Tudun Wada neighbourhood, which are occupied mainly by the indigenous Hausa, people typically live in traditional adobe compounds. The architecture of the wider city is varied, with clay buildings in the Hausa style standing beside modern multi-storey university and government buildings.

Zaria, first known as Zazzau, was the capital of the Hausa kingdom of Zazzau and one of the original seven Hausa city-states. Human settlement there is older than the kingdom: the region, like some of its neighbours, had sedentary Hausa settlement with institutional market exchange and farming. It was the most southern of the Hausa city-states, a destination for Saharan caravans and a prominent city in the Hausa slave trade. Islam arrived in the late 1450s by way of Kano and Katsina, and trade flourished as traders brought camel caravans of salt in exchange for slaves and grain.

The city-state's power peaked under Queen Amina, whose military campaigns established a tributary region that included the kingdoms of Kano and Katsina. At the end of the 16th century, after her death, Zaria came under the influence of the Jukun Kingdom and eventually became a tributary state itself. The Fulani captured it in 1805 during the Fulani Jihad. British forces led by Frederick Lugard took the city in 1901, and from 1914 to 1927 it was the break-of-gauge junction on the Bauchi Light Railway to the tin mines at Jos.

Zaria lies in Kaduna State and is the capital of the Zazzau Emirate Council and the home of the Emir of Zazzau. The 2006 census estimated its population at 736,000. Its economy rests mainly on agriculture, with guinea corn and millet as staples and cotton, groundnuts and tobacco as cash crops, and it is a market town and home to artisans in leather work, dyeing and cap making. For over 200 years it has been the centre of a textile industry making elaborately hand-embroidered robes worn by men throughout Nigeria and West Africa. It is the site of Ahmadu Bello University, the largest university in Nigeria, and holds a durbar festival at the Muslim feasts of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha.
zaydism: Zaydism, also called Fiver Shi'ism, is one of the three main branches of Shia Islam, the others being Twelverism and Ismailism, and is sometimes counted as a fifth school of Sunni law. It emerged in the eighth century after Zayd ibn Ali's unsuccessful rebellion against the Umayyad caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik. Most early Shia recognised Zayd's brother, Muhammad al-Baqir, as the fifth leader, but some regarded Zayd as the fifth imam, and these formed the Zaydi or Fiver offshoot.

Zaydis are typically considered the Shia branch closest to Sunni Islam. They regard rationalism as more important than Quranic literalism, and in Yemen they have historically been tolerant towards Shafi'i Sunnism. The classical form of Zaydism, called Hadawi, changed its stance towards Sunni and Shia traditions several times. The earliest form was Jarudiyya, and many of the first Zaydi states followed it.

Zaydi dynasties ruled in several regions. The Idrisid dynasty governed the western Maghreb from 788, and another Zaydi dynasty ruled in southern Spain in the 11th century. Under Hasan ibn Zayd the Alavids founded a Zaydi state in Daylam and Tabaristan in northern Iran in 864, which lasted until its leader was killed by the Sunni Samanids in 928. It was revived about forty years later in Daylam and Gilan and survived until 1126. The Karkiya dynasty ruled eastern Gilan from the 1370s to 1592, and the Zaydis of the Caspian region were forcibly converted to Twelver Shi'ism in the 16th century.

Around 893 al-Hadi ila'l-Haqq Yahya, a descendant of Hasan ibn Ali, established himself at Sa'dah in Yemen and founded the Rassid dynasty. The Zaydi imamate there was re-established under al-Mansur al-Qasim after an Ottoman invasion in the 16th century, and a new line began in the 19th century with Muhammad bin Yahya Hamid ad-Din. From the 15th century Zaydi doctrine merged gradually with elements of Shafi'i Sunnism, and by the mid-18th century the Qasimi imams had become a dynasty. These two lines ruled Yemen, with minor interruptions, until the Yemen Arab Republic was created in 1962.

Most of the world's Zaydis live in north-western Yemen and in Najran in Saudi Arabia. After the fall of the imamate in 1962 some Zaydis in northern Yemen converted to Sunni Islam, and the loss of imamic rule led a number of Zaydi scholars to call for its restoration. The North Yemen Civil War lasted from 1962 to 1970. Zaydi revivalist movements later arose from the discontent of the community.
zayed-bin-sultan-al-nahyan: Zayed was born at Qasr Al Hosn, Abu Dhabi, in 1918, the youngest of four sons of Sheikh Sultan bin Khalifa Al Nahyan, who ruled Abu Dhabi from 1922 until his death in 1926. He was named after his grandfather, Zayed the Great, who ruled from 1855 to 1909. At his birth Abu Dhabi was one of seven Trucial States on the lower coast of the Persian Gulf. After his father's death he moved to Al Ain, where no modern school existed on the coast. He received a basic instruction in Islam and lived in the desert among Bedouin tribesmen.

In 1946 Zayed became governor of the Eastern Region of Abu Dhabi, based at Al Ain, and he assisted the oil parties exploring there. When a small Saudi force occupied the village of Hamasa in the Buraimi Oasis in 1952, he opposed the Saudi claims and gave evidence at the arbitration tribunal in Geneva in September 1955. Oil was discovered in 1958 and exports began in 1962. Members of the ruling family, frustrated that Sheikh Shakhbut would not spend the revenue on development, asked for British help, and on 6 August 1966 Shakhbut was deposed in a bloodless palace coup and replaced by Zayed.

In January 1968 the British announced that they would end their treaties with the Trucial States and withdraw. On 18 February 1968 Zayed and Sheikh Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum of Dubai shook hands on the principle of founding a federation. After occasionally difficult negotiations with the other six rulers, the United Arab Emirates was formed in 1971, with Zayed as its president. He was re-elected in 1976, 1981, 1986 and 1991. In 1974 the Treaty of Jeddah settled the border dispute with Saudi Arabia.

Zayed used oil revenue to build hospitals, schools and universities, to which citizens had free access. In 1984 he financed the present dam at Ma'rib in Yemen. He died on 2 November 2004, aged 86, and was buried in the courtyard of the Grand Mosque in Abu Dhabi. His eldest son, Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan, succeeded him as ruler of Abu Dhabi and was ratified as president. Zayed is called Father of the Nation in the United Arab Emirates.
zealots: The word zealot translates the Hebrew kanai, meaning one who is zealous on behalf of God, and derives from the Greek zēlōtēs, an emulator or zealous admirer. Josephus used zealotry for a fourth sect or fourth Jewish philosophy beside the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes. He says it was founded by Judas of Galilee in 6 CE against the Census of Quirinius, and that its followers agreed with the Pharisees in other things but had an inviolable attachment to liberty and held that God was their only Ruler and Lord. Scholars note that the sources never clearly identify this fourth philosophy with the Zealots, and some argue the group was less clearly marked out before the war of 66 to 70 or 73.
At the core of zealotry was a total commitment to God's will and law, modelled on Phinehas, Elijah and the Hasmonean priest Mattathias. It was also driven by a belief in Israel's election by God.

The Zealots took a leading role in the First Jewish–Roman War, which lasted from 66 to 73 CE, objecting to Roman rule and seeking to remove it by force. Josephus, whose account is hostile, describes a murderous reign of terror in Jerusalem before the destruction of the Temple and says the Zealots followed John of Gischala. The group around Eleazar ben Simon is the only one known to have explicitly adopted the title. They held Jerusalem until 70, when Titus, the son of Emperor Vespasian, retook the city and destroyed Herod's Temple.

The Sicarii, who carried small daggers called sicae under their cloaks, were a distinct and rival faction with similar principles. Their leader early in the revolt was Menahem ben Judah, a descendant of Judas of Galilee. According to the historian Jonathan Price, the murder of Menahem and the expulsion of many of his followers in 66 was part of a struggle for control of the revolution in Jerusalem.

The Talmud calls the Zealots the Biryonim, meaning ruffians, and blames them for the fall of Jerusalem, citing their destruction of the city's stores of food and firewood during the siege. In the early 70s, Sicarii activists tried to raise rebellion in Egypt and Cyrenaica but were put down. Philip Alexander writes that the persistence of Zealot ideas prepared the way for the diaspora uprisings of 115 and the Bar Kokhba revolt of 132. Simon the Zealot appears among the apostles in the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles.
zeami-motokiyo: Zeami was born in 1363 near Nara and was known as Kiyomoto as a child. His father, Kan'ami Kiyotsugu, led a theatre troupe that performed mainly in the Kyoto region and grew popular in the late 1360s and early 1370s. Zeami acted in the troupe and was considered attractive and highly skilled. Ebina no Naami, an adviser of the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, booked the troupe to perform for the shogun, then 17 years old, who was impressed and became its patron. Under his support the troupe turned to entertainment rather than religious meaning, and the art became associated with the upper class.

Yoshimitsu invited Kan'ami and Zeami to court regularly, which proved controversial among aristocrats because of Zeami's lower-class background. The court statesman and poet Nijō Yoshimoto taught Zeami literature, poetry and philosophy, an unusual education for an actor.

Zeami received patronage in 1374, then an uncommon honour for an actor, and led the family troupe after his father's death in 1385. In 1394 he performed during Yoshimitsu's visit to the Kasuga shrine at Nara, and he gave two significant performances for the shogun in 1399. He competed with a rival Sarugaku actor, Inuo, for Yoshimitsu's favour. After Yoshimitsu died in 1408 the new shogun, Ashikaga Yoshimochi, preferred the dengaku work of Zoami, but Zeami kept patrons among the urban merchants and wrote a great deal between 1418 and 1428. In 1422 he became a lay monk.

Zeami drew on the Tale of the Heike and on Japanese and Chinese poetry, and used themes from Zen Buddhism. He wrote about twenty-one critical treatises over roughly four decades, the oldest known works on the philosophy of drama in Japanese literature. They dealt with the training of the actor, character acting, music and movement, and were meant for the troupe's members. They did not circulate widely until the 20th century. His shift from monomane towards yūgen may owe something to the influence of Doami.

Ashikaga Yoshinori became shogun in 1429 and turned hostile to Zeami. He admired Zeami's nephew Onnami and disagreed with Zeami's refusal to name him as his successor as head of the troupe. Possibly for this reason, though other explanations have been advanced, Yoshinori sent Zeami into exile on Sado Island. After Yoshinori's death in 1441 Zeami returned to the mainland and died in 1443. Plays universally attributed to him include Atsumori, Izutsu, Matsukaze, Takasago and Yamanba, and his plays have been handed down through generations of Kanze leaders.
zedekiah: Zedekiah, born Mattaniah, was the twentieth and last king of Judah. The Neo-Babylonian defeat of the Neo-Assyrian Empire at Nineveh in 612 BCE began the upheavals that destroyed the kingdom. King Josiah tried to block the Egyptian army marching north in 608 BCE and was mortally wounded at Megiddo. His son Jehoahaz was deposed after three months by the pharaoh Necho II in favour of an older brother, Jehoiakim. After the Babylonians defeated the Egyptians at Carchemish in 605 BCE, Nebuchadnezzar II besieged Jerusalem. Jehoiakim died during a later siege and was succeeded by his son Jeconiah, but Jerusalem fell within three months. Nebuchadnezzar deposed Jeconiah and installed his uncle Mattaniah, renamed Zedekiah.

According to the Hebrew Bible, Zedekiah was twenty-one when Nebuchadnezzar made him king in 597 BCE. A Babylonian chronicle agrees that its king captured the city of Judah and appointed a king of his own choice. Despite the strong remonstrances of the prophet Jeremiah, Baruch ben Neriah and others, Zedekiah allied with the Egyptian pharaoh Hophra and revolted. Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem for about thirty months. In the Book of Jeremiah, Zedekiah sends to the prophet for word from God, imprisons him in his palace, questions him in secret, and refuses his officials' demand to execute him while letting them throw him into a cistern. Ebed-melech then took thirty men to lift Jeremiah out.

Jerusalem fell in 587 or 586 BCE; scholars remain divided between the two years. According to the biblical accounts, Zedekiah and his followers tried to escape but were captured on the plains of Jericho and taken to Riblah, where he saw his sons put to death. His eyes were then put out, and he was carried in chains to Babylon, where he remained a prisoner until he died. Nebuchadnezzar sent Nebuzaradan to destroy Jerusalem, which was plundered and razed and its temple destroyed. Judah became the Babylonian province of Yehud, with Gedaliah ben Ahikam as governor; after Gedaliah was assassinated, most of the population fled to Egypt.
zeitz: Zeitz began as a Slavic pagan settlement that was later Christianized. It was first recorded under the Medieval Latin name Cici at the Synod of Ravenna in 967. The name is believed to derive from the Sorbian cica, meaning water or stream, for the White Elster. Between 965 and 982 it was the chief fortress of the March of Zeitz, and it was a bishop's residence from 968 until 1028, when the see moved to Naumburg. From the end of the 13th century the bishops again resided in their castle at Zeitz.

Swedish troops captured the town in the Thirty Years' War, and it was given to the Electorate of Saxony in 1644. It was the centre of Saxe-Zeitz until 1718, before returning to the Electorate, which became the Kingdom of Saxony in 1806. In 1815 it passed to the Kingdom of Prussia and became the district centre of the Merseburg region of the Province of Saxony, until 1944, when it joined the Province of Halle-Merseburg. The Herrmannsschacht, built in 1889, is one of the oldest brown coal briquette factories in the world. Zeitz was a county free city between 1901 and 1950.

The Brabag plant northeast of the town, a bombing target of the Oil Campaign of the Second World War, made synthetic fuel from lignite, with forced labour from the Wille subcamp of Buchenwald in Rehmsdorf and Gleina. United States troops occupied Zeitz on 27 April 1945, and it was transferred to Soviet control on 1 July 1945. On 18 August 1976 the Protestant clergyman Oskar Brüsewitz of Rippicha burnt himself to death in front of the Michaeliskirche as a protest against the East German system. After German reunification many local companies became uncompetitive, and 20,000 people lost their jobs or moved to other employment.

Zeitz lies on the White Elster, in the triangle formed by Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia and Saxony, and since 1 July 1994 it has belonged to the Burgenlandkreis district. Its sights lie mostly along the Romanesque Road. Schloss Moritzburg is a baroque castle with the cathedral of St. Peter and Paul, whose 10th-century crypt displays 17th-century tin coffins, among them that of Maurice, Duke of Saxe-Zeitz. The Michaeliskirche, dated 1154, was originally a Romanesque basilica and holds a 1517 original of Martin Luther's 95 Theses. The Gothic town hall dates from 1509 and was rebuilt in 1909.
zell-am-harmersbach: Zell am Harmersbach stands at the end of the Harmersbach Valley, a tributary valley of the Kinzig, in the Ortenaukreis between the Black Forest and the Rhine. The main castle of the Hohengeroldseck family at Biberach lies 8 km away, and Lahr, another Hohengeroldseck foundation, 16 km. The town includes the districts of Unterharmersbach, Unterentersbach and Oberentersbach, first mentioned in 1139, 1075 and 1111. Oberentersbach was administered from Zell until 1803. The districts joined the town in 1974 and 1975.

Zell was settled on land owned by Gengenbach Abbey, a monastery founded by the Lords of Geroldseck, whose sovereign lands covered much of the modern Ortenau district. In 1289 Rudolph I invested the monastery as an imperial abbey. The town separated from the abbey and from the authority of the Hohengeroldseck with the support of nearby Gengenbach and Offenburg, which had won imperial immediacy in 1366 and 1340. Zell obtained it toward the end of the 14th century.

The town suffered gravely in the Peasants War, the Thirty Years War and the wars of King Louis XIV of France. In 1800 the imperial city controlled about 50 square miles of territory. It bordered the Free City of Gengenbach on the west, the imperial abbey of Gengenbach on the north, the Imperial Valley of the Harmersbach on the east and the Lordship of Haslach, a Fürstenberg possession, on the south. The Final Recess (Reichsdeputationshauptschluss), ratified by Emperor Francis II on 27 April 1803, mediatized the city and annexed it to the Margrave of Baden.

The coat of arms, a black eagle on gold, is the crest of the Holy Roman Empire and recalls the town's imperial past. Museums include the Heimatmuseum in the Fürstenberger Hof, the Villa Haiss for contemporary art and the Storchenturm museum. The town is the birthplace of the Hahn und Henne (Rooster and Hens) pottery, and Karl Schaaff owned the Zeller porcelain factory from 1874 to 1907. The Harmersbach Valley Railway, 10.6 km long, is a branch of the Black Forest Railway. Zell is twinned with Baume-les-Dames in France and Frauenstein in Saxony.
zen: The word Zen comes from the Japanese pronunciation of the Middle Chinese word for meditation, itself derived from the Sanskrit dhyāna, which can be rendered as contemplation or a meditative state. The tradition developed in China during the Tang dynasty by blending Indian Mahayana Buddhism, particularly the Yogachara and Madhyamaka philosophies, with Chinese Taoist thought. It began as the Chan school, also called the Buddha-mind school. Tradition holds that it was brought to China by the monk Bodhidharma, an Indian or Central Asian figure.

Meditation practice first entered China through the translations of An Shigao and Kumārajīva (334–413 CE), who rendered dhyāna sutras based on the teaching of the Kashmiri Sarvāstivāda school. By the time of the Fifth Patriarch Hongren (601–674) the school was established as a separate school of Buddhism. Chan later spread south to Vietnam as Thiền, northeast to Korea as Seon and east to Japan as Zen.

Zen emphasises meditation, especially sitting meditation known as zazen in Japanese, and direct insight into one's own Buddha nature, called kenshō in Japanese. Its doctrine draws on the bodhisattva path, Madhyamaka, Yogachara, the Prajñāpāramitā literature and Buddha-nature texts such as the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra. Some sources describe it as a special transmission outside scriptures, yet masters such as Guifeng Zongmi and Jinul argued for the unity of Zen and the Buddhist teachings, and most Zen schools also keep chanting, precepts, ritual and scriptural study.

Two main lineages exist today: the Caodong tradition, traced to Dongshan Liangjie (807–869), and the Linji school, traced to Linji Yixuan, who died in 866. In the Song dynasty Caodong became associated with silent illumination, formulated by Hongzhi Zhengjue (1091–1157), while Linji became associated with Dahui Zonggao (1089–1163) and meditation on the huatou, the critical phrase of a koan. Teachers pass on lineages by dharma transmission from master to disciple.

Zen developed in a monastic setting, and most masters have been ordained monastics. East Asian monasteries stress self-sufficiency, so Zen monks do not live by begging but cook their own food and may farm. Japanese monks and nuns can marry after ordination because they ordain under the bodhisattva vows rather than the traditional monastic code. Intensive retreats called sesshin combine long sitting periods with formal meals and short periods of work.

Zen has also used the arts as training. Chan monk painters such as Guanxiu and Muqi Fachang communicated their understanding through brush painting and calligraphy, and calligraphy, poetry, gardening, flower arrangement and the tea ceremony have been used in practice. The Shaolin Monastery in Henan developed the first institutionalised form of gōngfu. The scholar Robert Sharf argues that seated meditation was less central to historical Zen monastery life than is often thought.
zengid-dynasty: The Zengids were a Turkoman Sunni Muslim dynasty that began as an atabegate of the Seljuk Empire created in 1127. After the murder of Aqsunqur al-Bursuqi, atabeg of Mosul, the Seljuk Empire named Zengi, son of Aq Sunqur al-Hajib, as the new atabeg of Mosul. He had been a successful Seljuk general in Iraq and governor of the whole region. Zengi became the chief Turkic potentate in northern Syria and Iraq, took Aleppo from the Artuqids in 1128 and captured the County of Edessa from the Crusaders in 1144. He was assassinated by a slave in 1146.

On Zengi's death his lands were divided. Mosul and Iraq went to his eldest son Saif ad-Din Ghazi I, and Aleppo and Edessa to his second son Nur ad-Din. Nur ad-Din defeated Raymond of Poitiers, Prince of Antioch, at Inab in 1149 and took Damascus from the Burid dynasty in 1154. After the death of the Seljuk ruler Ahmad Sanjar in 1157 the Zengids were nominally under Seljuk suzerainty but in practice independent. In the 1160s Nur ad-Din competed with Amalric of Jerusalem for control of Fatimid Egypt, where his commander Shirkuh campaigned from 1163 to 1169.

Nur ad-Din died on 15 May 1174, leaving his eleven-year-old son as-Salih Ismail. Saladin, who held Egypt as Nur ad-Din's governor, took Damascus in 1174 and Aleppo in 1183, ending Zengid rule in Syria. His siege of Mosul in 1182 and his later attack in 1185 both failed. A treaty of March 1186 left the Zengids in Mosul, obliged to supply the Ayyubids with military support when requested.

Like other atabegates, the Zengid army continued Seljuk traditions, combining professional troops and slave soldiers with mercenaries and Turcoman and Kurdish tribal auxiliaries. Bows were used extensively, and dense volleys could pierce armour or sometimes stop a Crusader charge. Mosul had a flourishing industry in the 13th century making luxury brass items inlaid with silver. Nur ad-Din rebuilt the walls of Aleppo and fortified its citadel, where several Crusaders were imprisoned, among them Joscelin II of Edessa, Raynald of Châtillon and Baldwin II.

Syriac Christianity remained active under the Zengids and went through a Syriac Renaissance, in which discriminatory rules against Christians were lifted, especially after 1174. Illustrated Gospel lectionaries were made near Mosul around 1220.
zeno-emperor: Zeno's original name was Tarasis, or more fully Tarasikodissa in his native Isaurian language, meaning Tarasis son of Kodissa. He was born in Isauria, at Rusumblada, a place later renamed Zenopolis in his honour. His mother was Lallis and he had a brother, Longinus. The Isaurians lived inland from the Mediterranean coast of Anatolia, in the Taurus Mountains, and the Romans regarded them as barbarians although they had been Roman subjects for over five centuries. Being Nicene Christians rather than Arians, they were not formally barred from the throne.

Zeno became an ally of Emperor Leo I, who saw the Isaurian general as a counterweight against the Germanic leader Aspar. In 466 he married Leo's daughter Ariadne, and they had a son, Leo. Ancient sources say that Tarasis took the Greek name Zeno when he married into the imperial family, after an earlier Isaurian officer, Flavius Zeno, who had fought against Attila in 447 and been consul.

Leo I died on 18 January 474 and the seven-year-old Leo II took the throne. Zeno was crowned co-emperor on 29 January and became sole emperor when the boy died the same year. He made an "eternal" peace with the Vandal king Genseric, but he was unpopular with the people and the Senate because of his origins. On 9 January 475 he fled Constantinople for Isauria after a plot by the dowager Empress Verina and her brother Basiliscus, who took the throne. Zeno regained it in 476 after Basiliscus lost support and the generals Illus and Armatus changed sides.

In the West, Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, acknowledging Zeno's suzerainty, and Zeno recognised Odoacer's rule in Italy. In the following years Zeno put down revolts by Marcianus and by Illus. He played the two Ostrogothic leaders, Theodoric the Amal and Theodoric Strabo, against each other, and after Strabo's death sent Theodoric to Italy, where he defeated Odoacer. In 482 he issued the Henotikon on the advice of Acacius, Patriarch of Constantinople, to reconcile Chalcedonians and Miaphysites. Pope Felix III condemned it and excommunicated Acacius in 484, which began the Acacian schism, lasting until 519.

Zeno died on 9 April 491, of dysentery or epilepsy, having ruled for seventeen years and two months. He left no son, and Ariadne chose a courtier, Anastasius I, to succeed him. His brother Longinus then revolted, which began the Isaurian War. The chroniclers Kedrenos and Zonaras later alleged that Ariadne had Zeno buried alive, but earlier and contemporary sources do not mention it and the tale is probably false.
zeno-of-citium: Zeno was born around 334 BCE at Citium in Cyprus, a city with both Phoenician and Greek inhabitants. Modern scholars disagree on whether to call him Phoenician, Greek or Greco-Phoenician. Most of what is known of his life comes from Diogenes Laërtius, writing in the 3rd century CE, whose anecdotes are generally considered unreliable. He reports that Zeno was a wealthy merchant, and that after a shipwreck on a voyage to Peiraeus he went to Athens, read Xenophon's Memorabilia in a bookshop and was pointed to Crates of Thebes as a man like Socrates.

Zeno is also said to have studied with the Megarian Stilpo, the dialecticians Diodorus Cronus and Philo, and Platonist philosophy under Xenocrates. He began teaching in the Stoa Poikile about 300 BCE, and his followers, first called Zenonians, came to be called Stoics.

Zeno divided philosophy into logic, physics and ethics. In physics he held that the universe is a divine reasoning being, in which an artisan-fire gives form to passive matter, and that it passes through regular cycles of formation and destruction. In ethics, happiness is a good flow of life, reached through right reason in agreement with the universal reason, the Logos. Unlike the Cynics, he allowed that things morally indifferent can have a relative value if they aid self-preservation.

None of his writings survives except in quotations. The best known, a Republic written in imitation of or opposition to Plato's, outlined an ideal Stoic society. A text found in Armenian in 1949 and attributed to him is by a Christian writer of about the late sixth century, now called Pseudo-Zeno.

Antigonus II Gonatas of Macedonia visited Zeno when in Athens. His pupils included Aristo of Chios, Sphaerus and Cleanthes, who succeeded him as head of the school. Diogenes says he declined Athenian citizenship so as not to seem unfaithful to his homeland.

Zeno died around 262 BCE; by Diogenes's account he tripped on leaving the school, broke a toe and died after holding his breath. He was honoured with a golden crown and a tomb. Because Chrysippus and others expanded his ideas, it is hard to know exactly what he thought. Stoicism flourished from the Hellenistic period through the Roman era.
zeno-of-elea: Zeno came from Elea, in what is now southern Italy, and little else about his life is known for certain. Plato portrays him in the dialogue Parmenides, set when Zeno is about 40 years old, as having once been a zealous defender of his teacher, wishing to show that belief in the physical world as it appears is more absurd than belief in the Eleatic single entity of existence. How accurate the portrayal is remains unknown, though it is agreed to bear some truth.

Zeno is known to have written one book, most likely in the 460s BCE, which in Plato's account he wrote in his youth and which was stolen and published without his permission. It is lost, and his thought is known through Plato, Aristotle, Diogenes Laertius and Simplicius of Cilicia.

Zeno was one of three major Eleatic philosophers, with Parmenides and Melissus of Samos. Where Melissus built on Parmenides, Zeno argued against opposing views, particularly the pluralism of the Pythagoreans. He was the first philosopher to use argumentative rather than descriptive language, writing paradoxes in the form of reductio ad absurdum. According to Proclus he had forty arguments against plurality.

Aristotle recorded four main paradoxes of motion in his Physics. The dichotomy holds that to cross a distance one must first cross half of it, and so on without end. Achilles and the tortoise holds that a swift runner can never catch a slow one who has a start. The arrow holds that an arrow in flight is stationary at any given instant.

Zeno died about 430 BCE. According to Diogenes Laertius he was killed while plotting to overthrow the tyrant Nearchus, and refused to name his fellow conspirators. He is said to have asked to whisper the names into Nearchus's ear, and to have bitten it and held on until he was killed.

Plato looked down on arguing from contradictions and thought Zeno did not take his arguments seriously, but Aristotle disagreed and answered the dichotomy with a distinction between actual and potential infinity. The Greek Atomists proposed the atom as a stopping point of division. Bertrand Russell credited the paradoxes with making possible the work of Karl Weierstrass.
zenobia: Zenobia bore the family name Septimia, and her native Palmyrene name was Bat-Zabbai, Aramaic for daughter of Zabbai. In Greek, the second language of Palmyra, she used the name Zenobia. Information about her ancestry is scarce and contradictory: nothing is known of her mother and her father's identity is debated. She was probably not a commoner. The Historia Augusta, whose details are of doubtful reliability, says she was fluent in Egyptian and Greek and spoke Latin, and claims descent from Cleopatra. This claim may have been invented by her enemies, but evidence suggests Zenobia herself made it, since a link with the Ptolemies would have given her a claim to Egypt.

Around 255, when she was about fourteen, she became the second wife of Odaenathus, lord of Palmyra. When the emperor Valerian was defeated and captured by the Persian king Shapur I in 260, Odaenathus was declared king of Palmyra. After successful campaigns against Persia he was crowned King of Kings of the East in 263 and governed the Roman territories from the Black Sea to Palestine.

Odaenathus and his eldest son were assassinated in 267. The army handed the crown to Zenobia's ten-year-old son Vaballathus within a day. She never claimed to rule in her own right and acted as his regent, but she held the real power, and Vaballathus was kept in her shadow. In 270 she launched an invasion that brought most of the Roman East under her sway and ended with the annexation of Egypt. By mid-271 her realm ran from Ancyra in central Anatolia to Upper Egypt, though she remained nominally subordinate to Rome.

In reaction to the campaign of the emperor Aurelian in 272, she declared her son emperor and took the title of empress, proclaiming Palmyra's independence. After heavy fighting the Romans were victorious. Aurelian captured her in late 272 as she tried to cross the Euphrates to Persia, and Palmyra capitulated soon after. She was described as a cultured monarch, tolerant towards her subjects, who kept a court open to scholars and philosophers.

Aurelian sent Zenobia and her son to Emesa for trial. No contemporary account of the trial survives, and the story of her cowardice comes from later hostile Roman sources and was probably Aurelian's propaganda. He executed most of his prisoners but spared her to be paraded in his triumph. Her fate after that is uncertain, and ancient historians leave conflicting accounts. She is a patriotic symbol in Syria, and her rise and fall have inspired historians, artists and novelists.
zerbst: Zerbst lies in the district of Anhalt-Bitterfeld in Saxony-Anhalt. Its town centre stands on the river Nuthe about 13 km northeast of the Elbe, halfway between Magdeburg and Wittenberg. Until an administrative reform in 2007 it was the capital of the former district of Anhalt-Zerbst. In the 8th century the area east of the Elbe was settled by Polabian Slavs, and the town was named Serbst after them, which developed into Zerbst.

The area was incorporated about 937 into the Gau Ciervisti of the Saxon Eastern March in the course of the German eastward settlement. It is not clear when Zerbst was founded, but the name Ciervisti, mentioned as early as 949, may already refer to a fortified Slavic settlement. Thietmar of Merseburg recorded a town as Zirwisti urbs in 1018. In the early 12th century the Ascanian ruler Albert the Bear had the fortress rebuilt, and the settlement was first fortified with town walls about 1250.

In 1307 Prince Albert I of Anhalt acquired the town from the Barby comital family, beginning centuries of rule by the House of Anhalt. In 1375 Zerbster Bitterbier was first mentioned, and by the Middle Ages the town had 600 breweries.

After the Reformation Zerbst became a Calvinist centre, and the Francisceum Gymnasium Illustre was an important Calvinist college from 1582 to 1798. From 1603 to 1793 it was the residence of the princes of Anhalt-Zerbst, whose rule also included the Lordship of Jever in East Frisia. The Baroque composer Johann Friedrich Fasch lived there from 1722 to 1758 as court composer and later Kapellmeister, and Fasch Festivals have been held in the city since 1983. In 1745 Princess Sophie Auguste Friederike of Anhalt-Zerbst married Peter, the heir to the Russian throne. As Catherine II she herself reigned as empress from 1762 to 1796. In 1797 Zerbst became part of the Principality of Anhalt-Dessau.

In the later part of the Second World War a labour camp was set up at the edge of the military airfield, where about 700 inmates classed as part Jewish in Nazi terms did hard labour. On 16 April 1945 some eighty percent of Zerbst was destroyed in an Allied air raid. The old town was rebuilt in the following decades, which fundamentally changed the townscape, as only a few historical structures were preserved or reconstructed. The town, with about 24,000 inhabitants, covers a large area after the incorporation of 21 communities in 2010.
zerubbabel: Zerubbabel is documented only in the Hebrew Bible. His name, from the Akkadian for seed of Babylon, shows how quickly the exiled elite took on Babylonian ways. He was a grandson of Jeconiah, the penultimate king of Judah, and belonged to the main Davidic line through Solomon, though Jeremiah had said that no offspring of Jeconiah would sit on the throne. Texts disagree on his father. Ezra, Nehemiah and Haggai call him son of Shealtiel, while the Masoretic Text of 1 Chronicles makes him a son of Shealtiel's brother Pedaiah. That reading may be a scribal error in a garbled passage.

According to the Book of Ezra, Zerubbabel led the first group of exiles, numbering 42,360, back from Babylon in the first year of Cyrus the Great. The date is generally thought to lie between 538 and 520 BCE. He is always named with the high priest Joshua, son of Jozadak, and together they began rebuilding the Temple, Zerubbabel descended from David and Joshua from Aaron. Darius I appointed him governor of Yehud, and the work began in Darius's second year, 520 BCE. It has been suggested that revolts at the start of Darius's reign left him free to begin it.

The prophets Haggai and Zechariah gave unclear oracles about his authority. Haggai records God saying he would wear him like a signet ring, words often read as messianic. The Book of Ezra begins with Sheshbazzar, also called governor, who then vanishes from the story. Explanations include that they were the same man, that Sheshbazzar was his uncle, or that Sheshbazzar began the work and Zerubbabel finished it. Zerubbabel appears in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew and Luke, in the tale of three guardsmen before Darius in 1 Esdras, and in the seventh-century Apocalypse of Zerubbabel.
zeus: The earliest attested forms of the god's name are the Mycenaean Greek di-we and di-wo, written in the Linear B syllabic script. In addition to his Indo-European inheritance, the classical cloud-gatherer takes certain iconographic traits, such as the scepter, from the cultures of the ancient Near East. The Greeks equated Zeus with many foreign weather gods, which allowed Pausanias to remark that it is a saying common to all men that Zeus is king in heaven. In ancient Rome he was identified with the god Jupiter.

In Hesiod's Theogony, composed about 730 to 700 BCE, the Titan Cronus swallows each of his children at birth after a prophecy that one of them will overthrow him. Rhea gives birth to Zeus, the youngest, at Lyctus in Crete. Other sources say that nymphs nursed him in a cave, feeding him on the milk of the she-goat Amalthea, while the Kouretes beat their spears on their shields to hide the infant's cries. When he reached manhood Cronus was made to disgorge the children he had swallowed. Zeus freed the Cyclopes, who gave him the thunderbolt, and the Olympians led by Zeus then fought the Titans in the Titanomachy.

Zeus, Poseidon and Hades divided the cosmos, Zeus receiving the sky, Poseidon the sea and Hades the underworld. In Hesiod's version Zeus's first wife was Metis, whom he swallowed when she was about to bear Athena, who then emerged from his head, and his last wife was his sister Hera. Authors also describe numerous affairs with mortal women, in which he often changes his form, as when he takes the shape of a bull to carry Europa to Crete.
