In the Iliad he plays a major part in the Trojan War.

Popular conceptions of Zeus differed widely from place to place. Local varieties had little in common beyond the name, exercised different areas of authority and were worshipped in different ways, and some cults treated him as an earth god rather than a sky god. They were gradually merged, through conquest and religious syncretism, with the Homeric conception, and local forms were distinguished by epithets. The major centre where all Greeks gathered to honour him was Olympia, whose quadrennial festival included the Games and where an altar was made not of stone but of ash from the remains of many centuries of sacrificed animals. Elsewhere he was worshipped, for example, as Zeus Aetnaeus on Mount Aetna.
zhang-jinghui: Zhang Jinghui was born on 21 June 1871 in Tai'an, south-west of Mukden in Liaoning Province, an area that became a battlefield in the First Sino-Japanese War. At an early age he joined the Honghuzi irregular cavalry of the Manchurian warlord Zhang Zuolin, forces that the Japanese recruited as mercenaries during the Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905. When Yuan Shikai died in 1916 the Beiyang Army split into mutually hostile factions.

Zhang Jinghui deserted Zhang Zuolin for the Zhili clique of Wu Peifu, but later rejoined him. He served as minister of war in the Beiyang Government from May 1926 to June 1927 and as minister of industry in the National Pacification Army Government from June 1927 to June 1928, and was then appointed governor of the Harbin and China Eastern Railway Special District in northern Manchuria. After Zhang Zuolin was killed in the Huanggutun Incident on 4 June 1928, his relations with the son and successor, Zhang Xueliang, deteriorated.

Following the Mukden Incident and the invasion of Manchuria by the Japanese Kwantung Army in 1931, Zhang called a conference on 27 September to form an emergency committee aiming at the secession of Manchuria from China. He proclaimed his territory self-governing and was inaugurated as governor on 7 January 1932. He then came to terms with Japan and accepted the governorship of Heilongjiang Province in Manchukuo. His refusal to leave Harbin for Qiqihar caused friction with the Kwantung Army, and he was set aside when General Ma Zhanshan accepted the post on 14 February 1932. Ma revolted in April, and Zhang replaced him as minister of defence.

His appointment as prime minister on 21 May 1935 was made at the instigation of the Kwantung Army and over the objections of Emperor Puyi. He is said to have spent his days copying Buddhist sutras and was nicknamed the Tofu Prime Minister in his own lifetime. He is recorded as speaking out against the Japanese administration only once, to criticise the forced sale of land to Japanese colonists. In 1943 he represented Manchukuo at the Greater East Asia Conference in Tokyo; in the same year Time magazine published a false report that he had killed his family and his Japanese adviser and then himself.

After the war the Soviet Union held him in Siberia until 1950, when he was extradited to the People's Republic of China and imprisoned at the Fushun War Criminals Management Centre. He died there of heart failure on 11 January 1959.
zhangjiakou: Zhangjiakou lies in north-western Hebei, bordering Beijing to the southeast and Inner Mongolia to the north and west. Since ancient times it has been a stronghold of military significance, and it is nicknamed the Northern Gate of Beijing. Dajingmen, an important gate and junction of the Great Wall, is located there. The urban area is surrounded by mountains on three sides, and the Qingshui River divides it into two districts, Qiaodong and Qiaoxi. The name means pass of the Zhang family. It is a clipping of Zhangjiakoubu, the earthwork fortress of the Zhang family, named for the Ming official Zhang Wen, who began fortifying the city in 1429. Europeans long knew it as Kalgan, from the Mongolian name Qaɣalɣan, meaning barrier or gate.

The region was a battleground in the Han–Xiongnu wars, and the Qin general Meng Tian joined the Great Walls of Yan, Qin and Zhao near here. In the Ming dynasty the garrison of Xuanfu, one of the Nine Garrisons, grew to 151 thousand troops between 1403 and 1424. In 1449 the Emperor Yingzong of Ming was captured by pursuing Mongol troops in Huailai County, an event called the Tumu Crisis. In 1571 Altan Khan received a title from the Longqing Emperor and agreed a lasting peace, after which Zhangjiakou changed from a military base into an important horse market for Mongolian mounts.

It was the chief northern gate for Europeans travelling along the Northern Tea Road, among them Ivan Petlin in 1619. From 1727 it was an important station in the Kyakhta trade between Russia and China, and in autumn long lines of camels carried tea chests from Zhangjiakou across the Gobi to Kyakhta. In the 19th century the town had an estimated 70–100,000 people, and some Russian merchants had permanent residences and warehouses outside the gate.

The Beijing–Zhangjiakou Railway, the first railway designed and built solely by Chinese, with Zhan Tianyou as chief engineer, connected it to Beijing in October 1909. The Japanese occupied the region in 1937 and made Kalgan the capital of the autonomous province of South Chahar, and a Federated Mengjiang Commission supervised the economy of Japanese-occupied Inner Mongolia.

Zhangjiakou is a prefecture-level city, with 4,118,908 people at the census of 2020. It is a gateway between Hebei, Inner Mongolia and Beijing, and has a notable wine industry at Huailai. It hosted skiing and snowboarding events of the 2022 Winter Olympics at Taizicheng in Chongli District.
zhangye: Zhangye lies in the centre of the Hexi Corridor, in central Gansu, and its urban core, Ganzhou, stands in the oasis formed by the Ruo or Hei River. The area is on the frontier of China proper, protecting it from the nomads of the northwest and giving its armies access to the Tarim Basin. The city takes up the entire breadth of the province, from Inner Mongolia on the north to Qinghai on the south. Its streams, sunlight and fertile soil made it an important agricultural centre. Ganzhou was named for the sweet waters of its oasis, and Marco Polo's Travels gives the name as Campichu.

Zhangye Commandery was established by the Western Han in 111 BCE, with its seat at the site of modern Wuwei. The meaning of the name Zhangye is unclear; one popular theory reads it as Extending Arm, from a phrase in the Han Shu about extending the arm of the country through to the Western Realm. During the Western Han, Han armies often fought the Xiongnu in this area, and it was an important outpost on the Silk Road. Before being overrun by the Mongols it was dominated by the Western Xia dynasty, and earlier by the Uyghurs, from at least the early 10th century. Its relation to the larger Uyghur state of Qocho is obscure, but it may have been a vassal.

Kublai, the founder of the Yuan dynasty, is said to have been born in the Dafo Temple in Zhangye, now the site of the longest wooden reclining Buddha in China. Marco Polo's journal states that he spent a year in the town on his journey to China. In the 1880s a Qing official in charge of erecting poles for the telegraph network ordered the pine forests of the Babao Mountains cleared. They had regulated the flow of the Ruo River by ensuring that melt-waters lasted through the summer, and afterwards the region became prone to flooding in summer and drought in autumn. Christian missionaries arrived in 1879, after Suzhou, modern Jiuquan, was found too hostile.

Zhangye is a prefecture-level city with 1,131,016 permanent residents at the census of 2020, and 26 ethnic minorities besides the Han are represented, including many Hui, Yugur and Tibetans. The Zhangye Danxia National Geological Park, known for its colourful rock formations, lies 30 km west of the city centre. The Lanzhou–Xinjiang Railway runs through the city.
zhanjiang: Zhanjiang is a prefecture-level city that administers the entire Leizhou Peninsula and lies directly opposite Haikou, the capital of Hainan, across the Qiongzhou Strait. It is the southernmost port on the coast of mainland China and a centre of commerce and navigation for much of south-western China. The city sits on an inlet of the South China Sea, southwest of Guangzhou, and its climate is humid subtropical, with heavy rain from April to September.

During the Qin dynasty the area belonged to the Xiang Shire administrative division, and under the Han dynasty Xuwen County was set up as the seat for the whole Leizhou Peninsula. The port became one of the earliest departure points on the Maritime Silk Road. In the Song dynasty many Putian (Hinghwa) colonists settled in the region, later forming the ethnolinguistic majority of the peninsula, alongside the Baiyue, Cantonese, Tanka and foreign merchants.

In 1898 the area was a small fishing port when the French established control and forced China to lease a 99-year concession called Guangzhouwan. Much of the local population had fled, so Cantonese peasants from north of Leizhou were brought in, which made Yue Chinese the dominant local language. The French developed the port as Fort Bayard, intending it as a logistical centre for their concessions in southern China, though poverty and underdevelopment limited the effort. They held the enclave until 1943, when Japan occupied it during World War II. After the war it was briefly returned to France before being ceded to China. The Republic of China renamed the area Zhanjiang, a variant of Zhanchuan, the name of an earlier county.

After the People's Republic of China was established in 1949 the city grew in strategic and economic importance, and by 1957 it had a modern deep-water port able to handle ships of up to 50,000 tons. In 1984, under Deng Xiaoping's policy of reform and opening-up, it was designated an open city to attract foreign investment. In the early 1990s a rail line linked it to Guangzhou and was later extended to Hai'an at the southern tip of the peninsula.

The 2020 census counted a resident population of 6,981,236. Leizhou Min is the prestige language in several districts, Yue Chinese is spoken in Potou District and other areas settled in the French period, and Hakka is spoken in Lianjiang County. The local Leizhou Opera has a history of over 300 years. Zhanjiang is the headquarters of the South Sea Fleet of the People's Liberation Army Navy. Its port is a natural deep-water harbour protected by three outer islands, and the old French quarter in Chikan survives as Chikan Old Street, with arched windows, balconies and tiled roofs.
zhaoqing: Zhaoqing lies 110 km west of Guangzhou, in the west of the Pearl River Delta, on the north shore of the Xi River, which flows from west to east. Gaoyao stands opposite on the south bank. A plain lies to the south and west of the city, with mountains to the east and north. Its name, meaning Beginning Auspiciousness, was bestowed on the area by Emperor Huizong of the Song in 1118. Earlier it was known to the Qin as Sihui and to the Han as Gaoyao, and under the Sui it was renamed Duanzhou as the seat of Duan Prefecture.

In the late 6th and early 7th centuries the administration moved from Gaoyao to Duanzhou on the opposite bank, which became an important administrative and military centre of the southern Sui Empire. The city wall was built in Duanzhou during the reign of Emperor Renzong of Song (1022–1063).

When the Portuguese arrived in the 16th century Zhaoqing was still an important centre, the seat of the Viceroy of Liangguang, meaning Guangdong and Guangxi. In 1582 the Italian Jesuit Michele Ruggieri came from Macao, sent in place of the governor and bishop whom the viceroy Chen Rui had summoned. After several false starts he and Matteo Ricci were allowed to settle in the city, in the first Jesuit mission house on mainland China, after the governor Wang Pan learned of Ricci's skill as a mathematician and cartographer.

Ricci drew the first modern Chinese map of the world in Zhaoqing in 1584. Ruggieri left for Rome in 1588, and Ricci was expelled by a new viceroy the next year, which obliged the Jesuits to move to Shaozhou, now Shaoguan.

In the fall of the Ming in the mid-17th century Zhaoqing was the capital of the Southern Ming resistance of the Prince of Gui, who styled himself the Yongli Emperor. The town fell in 1650 and the prince moved to Guilin and then to places in Guangxi, Yunnan and Kokang. The Jesuits Andreas Wolfgang Koffler and later Michał Boym stayed for some time at his court. Under the Qing the viceroy moved to Guangzhou, but Zhaoqing remained the seat of a commandery.

Once one of the most important cities of southern China, Zhaoqing lost that standing under the Qing dynasty. It has six National Key Cultural Relic Protection Sites, among them the Song city walls, the Seven Star Crags carvings and the Yuejiang Tower in Duanzhou District. Dinghu Mountain, beside the Seven Star Crags, was the first nature reserve established in China.
zhejiang: Zhejiang is a coastal province of East China, bordered by Jiangsu and Shanghai to the north, Anhui to the northwest, Jiangxi to the west and Fujian to the south, with the East China Sea to the east. Hills account for about 70 per cent of its area, rising towards the south and west, and the highest peak, Huangmaojian Peak, reaches 1,929 metres. It has a longer coastline than any other mainland province and about three thousand islands, the most in China. The Qiantang River, formerly the Zhe River, gives the province its name. Hangzhou stands at the end of the Grand Canal on Hangzhou Bay.

The Kuahuqiao settlement near Hangzhou dates from 6000 to 5000 BCE, and the Neolithic Hemudu culture began in 5500 BCE and the Liangzhu culture in 3400 BCE. In the second millennium BCE the area lay outside the main sphere of Shang civilisation and was populated by peoples known as the Dongyue. The Kingdom of Yue controlled it in the Spring and Autumn period, and the Qin dynasty annexed it in 222 BCE. Kuaiji Commandery was the power base of Xiang Liang and Xiang Yu in their rebellion against the Qin.

Qiantang, the former name of Hangzhou, was one of three major southern centres that supplied tax revenue to the north in the Six Dynasties period, and in 589 it was raised in status and renamed Hangzhou. As the heartland of the Jiangnan, Zhejiang was the wealthiest area under the Six Dynasties, Sui and Tang, and its grain and resources travelled north along the Grand Canal that the Sui restored and expanded. After the Tang fell in 907, King Qian Liu established the kingdom of Wuyue, with Hangzhou as its capital. The Song annexed it around 960. In 1127 Hangzhou became the Song capital under the name Lin'an, noted for its prosperity and beauty and suspected to have been the largest city in the world.

The Mongols occupied the province in the late 13th century and merged it with neighbouring provinces, and the present-day province was established in 1368. In the late Ming and Qing periods its ports were centres of international trade. During the Second World War much of Zhejiang was occupied. After the Doolittle Raid, the Imperial Japanese Army began the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Campaign against locals who had helped downed American airmen; at least 10,000 civilians died in Jiangxi.

Zhejiang has a population of about 64.6 million, and its capital and largest city is Hangzhou, with Ningbo, Yiwu and Wenzhou also notable. Hangzhou includes the West Lake. Various varieties of Chinese are spoken, the most prominent being Wu Chinese. The province is the birthplace of Chiang Kai-shek.
zhelyu-zhelev: Zhelev was born on 3 March 1935 into a modest village family in Veselinovo in north-eastern Bulgaria. He studied philosophy at Sofia University, graduating in 1958 and gaining a PhD in 1974. A member of the Bulgarian Communist Party, he was expelled from it for political reasons in 1965. All employment in Bulgaria was state-regulated, so he was unemployed for six years, a condition termed social parasitism in communist terminology. He spent much of that time in virtual internal exile in his wife's village, scraping a living from odd jobs on farms.

In 1982 Zhelev published his book Fascism. Three weeks after publication it was removed from bookstores and libraries throughout the country, because its description of the fascist states of Italy, Germany and Spain made these regimes comparable to the Communist regimes of the Eastern Bloc. In 1988 he founded the Ruse Committee, and in 1989 he became a founding member and chairman of the Club for Support of Openness and the Reform. This helped him to the chairmanship of the Coordinating Council of the Union of Democratic Forces. He was one of the most prominent figures of the 1989 Bulgarian Revolution, which ended the 35-year rule of Todor Zhivkov.

Zhelev was elected a member of parliament in June 1990 to the 7th Grand National Assembly, whose main task was to draft a new democratic constitution. After President Petar Mladenov resigned, the Assembly elected Zhelev his successor on 1 August 1990, the first head of state in 44 years who was neither a Communist nor a fellow traveller. The constitution of July 1991 provided for direct election of the president, for at most two terms, and made the office largely representative.

In the first such election, in January 1992, he led the first round on 12 January and won the runoff a week later against Velko Valkanov, backed by the Socialists, with 52.8% of the votes. He suspended his membership in the Union of Democratic Forces, believing the presidency should be above politics. In 1996 he lost the party's nomination for a second term to Petar Stoyanov.

After his presidency ended in 1997 Zhelev became honorary chair of the Liberal Democratic Union and of Liberal International and set up a foundation named after him. He also founded and presided over the Balkan Political Club, a union of former political leaders from Southeast Europe. He died in Sofia on 30 January 2015, aged 79.
zheng-he: Zheng He was born Ma He into a Muslim, Hui, family of Kunyang, Kunming, in Yunnan, then ruled by the Principality of Liang, which was loyal to the Northern Yuan dynasty. He was a great-great-great-grandson of Sayyid Ajjal Shams al-Din Omar, who governed Yunnan in the early Yuan period, and his grandfather and father bore the title hajji. The Ming armies captured him in Yunnan in 1381. He was castrated and enslaved as a eunuch servant in the household of Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, who later became the Yongle Emperor.

Ma He took part in the prince's campaigns against the Mongols, assisted him in the Jingnan campaign that overthrew the Jianwen Emperor in 1402, and took the surname Zheng, conferred by the Yongle Emperor. Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming government sponsored seven naval expeditions under his command, with Wang Jinghong as second in command. The Yongle Emperor designed them to establish a Chinese presence, impose imperial control over the Indian Ocean trade and extend the tributary system. The first voyage left Suzhou on 11 July 1405 with a fleet of 317 ships carrying almost 28,000 crewmen. The Xuande Emperor commissioned the last voyages.

One theory holds that Zheng He died in 1433, during or shortly after his seventh voyage, probably at Calicut. Another has him continuing as defender of Nanjing and dying in 1435. His tomb in Nanjing is a cenotaph believed to contain his clothes and headgear. In the decades after the last voyage imperial officials minimised the expeditions in the official histories. His voyages became well known in China and abroad after Liang Qichao's biography of 1904, and the Chinese diaspora in Southeast Asia venerates him, often under the alias Sam Po.
zhengzhou: Zhengzhou lies in north-central Henan, on the southern bank of the Yellow River, at the eastern foothills of the Xiong'er Mountains where the river's valley widens into the North China Plain. It borders Luoyang to the west, Kaifeng to the east and Xinxiang to the northeast. The city stands at the crossing of the north–south route skirting the Taihang Mountains and the mountains of western Henan. Its prefecture covers 7,567 km2, of which the city centre occupies 709.69 km2. It lies in the Zhongyuan region, an area inhabited continuously for over 4,000 years and regarded as a cradle of Chinese civilization.

Several city ruins from the early Shang dynasty have been found in the Zhengzhou area, including candidate sites for the early Shang capitals Ao, Bo or Yan. Since 1950 excavations at Zhengzhou Shang City, near the historical centre of the modern city, have provided evidence of Shang settlement around 1600 BCE. About 20 km to the northwest, remains of large public buildings and a complex of small settlements have been found at a site that some identify as the Shang capital of Ao. Parts of the Shang city wall, built some 3,600 years ago, still stand in the downtown.

After the Shang the area remained an important regional city because of its position on the North China Plain. The settlement was first known as Guancheng, the city of the Guan family, who held it as a city-state. It later became the seat of a prefecture under the Sui dynasty, and the character Zheng in its modern name refers to the Zheng state that once governed the region. In June 1938, during the Second Sino-Japanese War, Nationalist forces breached the dikes at Huayuankou, north of Zhengzhou, to slow the Japanese advance. The flood inundated large areas of Henan, Anhui and Jiangsu, and the Yellow River did not return to its original course until 1947.

Zhengzhou is the capital and largest city of Henan, with a population of about 12.6 million in the 2020 census. It is a main national transport hub, and it has been a major industrial city of the People's Republic since 1949, with textiles as its staple industry. The Zhengzhou Commodity Exchange, approved by the State Council in October 1990, was the first futures exchange in China. The Zhengzhou Confucius Temple, first built in the Eastern Han dynasty, is among the oldest Confucian temples in China. About 90 km southwest, in Dengfeng, the Shaolin Monastery and its Pagoda Forest were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.
zhou-dynasty: In Chinese tradition the Zhou lineage began with Qi, the Lord of Millet (Houji), a culture hero credited with improving agriculture. Later chiefs settled at Bin and then moved to Zhou in the Wei River valley, which remained their heartland. Wen moved the capital to Feng, and his son Wu, with his ally Jiang Ziya, led an army of 45,000 men and 300 chariots across the Yellow River and defeated the Shang king Di Xin at the Battle of Muye. The Zhou made a member of the Shang royal family Duke of Song and appear to have spoken a language much like the Shang's.

King Wu died early, leaving a young heir, and the Duke of Zhou assisted his nephew King Cheng. When the Three Guards, Zhou princes stationed in the east, rebelled with Shang partisans, the Duke put them down and extended the kingdom eastward. He set up the fengjian system of hereditary fiefs and expounded the Mandate of Heaven. Over generations the kinship ties between the kings and the regional lords thinned, and peripheral states gained power on par with the Zhou.

In 771 BCE the Quanrong, joined by the Marquis of Shen, whose daughter King You had demoted as queen, sacked the capital Haojing and killed You. Nobles declared the marquis's grandson King Ping and moved the capital east to Wangcheng. Royal authority then declined. The court recognised Han, Zhao and Wei as independent states in 403 BCE, and in 344 BCE Duke Hui of Wei was the first to claim the title of king. Qin captured Wangcheng in 256 BCE and killed King Nan, traditionally the last Zhou king.

The Mandate of Heaven held that Heaven gave power to the one ruler who upheld harmony, and withdrew it from a king whose people suffered. The Zhou used it to justify replacing the Shang. Farming was done mainly by ordinary rural households owing labour, taxes and military service, with slaves a minority. Five ranks of nobility stood below the king: duke, marquis, count, viscount and baron.

The Zhou period is often seen as the high point of Chinese bronze casting, and in the Eastern Zhou the Hundred Schools of Thought arose, including Confucianism, Taoism, Mohism and Legalism. The ritual system called li was later set down in texts compiled under the Han.
zhou-enlai: Zhou was born on 5 March 1898 in Huai'an, Jiangsu, and studied at the Nankai Middle School in Tianjin. His Chinese biography makes him a leader of the Tianjin student protests of the May Fourth Movement, but many modern scholars think it unlikely that he took part. In 1924 he returned from Europe to join the Whampoa Military Academy at Guangzhou as its chief political officer, and he married Deng Yingchao on 8 August 1925.

After the split between Nationalists and Communists in 1927 he went underground. From 1929 he built a network of Communist cells in Shanghai, changing residence at least once a month. In the Jiangxi Soviet he reorganised the Red Army, and when the Communists abandoned it he organised the logistics of the withdrawal that became the Long March. In 1936 he helped bring about the Xi'an Incident through contact with Zhang Xueliang. During the war against Japan he led the Communist liaison office at the Nationalist capital, first at Wuhan and then at Chongqing.

After the People's Republic of China was proclaimed on 1 October 1949, Zhou became Premier and Minister of Foreign Affairs, holding the second post until 1958. He became the architect of early foreign policy. He cultivated Jawaharlal Nehru and helped formalise the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence from the 1954 Sino-Indian Agreement. At the Geneva Conference of 1954 he was credited with helping the powers reach the agreement ending the Indochina War, and at the Bandung Conference of 1955 he spoke for peace and the abolition of nuclear arms.

During the Cultural Revolution he was the main force keeping the government and economy running. He tried to protect scientists, academics and artists, though he could not shelter most officials in the institutions he controlled. After the fall of Lin Biao he was elected first-ranking Vice Chairman of the Party in 1973.

Zhou withdrew from public life after 13 January 1975 and died on 8 January 1976. He had willed that his ashes be scattered over the hills and rivers of his hometown, so there was no burial ceremony. After a single memorial on 15 January, further public mourning was prohibited. On 4 April 1976 thousands gathered at the Monument to the People's Heroes in Tiananmen Square to commemorate him, and some slogans attacked the Gang of Four and even Mao.
He has been remembered as a skilled negotiator and a pragmatic statesman. Deng Xiaoping held that without him the Cultural Revolution might have been worse, but might not have lasted as long.
zhu-wen: Zhu Wen was born on 5 December 852, the youngest of three sons of Zhu Cheng, an instructor in the Five Classics in Dangshan County. His father died while he was a boy, and his mother took her sons to the household of Liu Chong of Xiao County. He formed a bandit gang and in about 877 joined the rebel army of Huang Chao. After Huang Chao took the capital Chang'an in January 881, Zhu received a separate command and captured Tong Prefecture.

By 882 Huang Chao was effectively surrounded. Zhu surrendered to the Tang governor Wang Chongrong. Emperor Xizong of Tang rewarded him with a command and a new name, Quanzhong, wholeheartedly loyal. On 3 May 883 he was appointed military governor of Xuanwu Circuit at Bian Prefecture, the modern Kaifeng. In spring 884 he and Li Keyong, chief of the Shatuo Turks, routed Huang Chao's generals. On the night of 11 June 884 Zhu tried to have Li Keyong assassinated, which began a struggle of forty years between their houses.

He destroyed rival warlords such as Qin Zongquan, Shi Pu, Zhu Xuan and Zhu Jin. In 902 he besieged Li Maozhen at Fengxiang, where Emperor Zhaozong of Tang was held, and in 903 Li Maozhen handed the emperor over; all the palace eunuchs were then slaughtered. In spring 904 Zhu forced the emperor, his household and the people of Chang'an to move to Luoyang. That autumn he had Emperor Zhaozong murdered and a child, Emperor Ai of Tang, enthroned. Nine of the dead emperor's sons were killed, and some 30 senior officials of aristocratic family were forced to commit suicide at Baima and their bodies thrown into the Yellow River.

The deposed Emperor Ai was made Prince of Jiyin and poisoned in 908. Most circuits submitted to the new emperor, but the realms of Li Keyong, Li Maozhen, Yang Wo and Wang Jian did not. A siege of the Jin city of Lu was broken in 908 by Li Keyong's son Li Cunxu, and in spring 911 the Later Liang army was crushed at Boxiang.

The histories describe him as violent towards his subordinates and say that he raped the wives of his officers and of his own sons. In summer 912, gravely ill, he meant to leave the throne to his adoptive son Zhu Youwen and ordered another son, Zhu Yougui, away from the capital. Fearing execution, Zhu Yougui led imperial guards into the palace and killed him on 18 July 912.
zhu-xi: Zhu Xi was born in Fujian on 18 October 1130, where his father worked as subprefectural sheriff. His family originated in Wuyuan County, Huizhou, in modern Jiangxi province. After his father was forced from office in 1140 for opposing the government's appeasement policy towards the Jurchen, Zhu Xi was taught at home by him. When his father died in 1143, he studied with his father's friends Hu Xian, Liu Zihui and Liu Mianzhi. In 1148, at the age of 19, he passed the imperial examination and became a presented scholar (jinshi). From 1153 he studied under Li Tong, who followed the Neo-Confucian tradition of Cheng Hao and Cheng Yi, and he became Li's formal student in 1160.

Zhu Xi's first official post was Subprefectural Registrar of Tong'an, from 1153 to 1156. He then held no office until 1179, when he was appointed Prefect of Nankang Military District and revived the White Deer Grotto Academy. Three years later he was demoted for attacking the incompetence and corruption of some influential officials. After his last dismissal he was accused of numerous crimes and a petition was made for his execution, with much of the opposition led by the Prime Minister Han Tuozhou, a political rival. He wrote, compiled and edited almost a hundred books and taught groups of students, many of whom studied under him for years.

Rather than concentrating on the I Ching as other Neo-Confucians did, Zhu Xi emphasised the Four Books: the Great Learning, the Doctrine of the Mean, the Analects and the Mencius. His commentaries on them were not widely recognised in his time but later became the standard ones, and from 1313 to 1905 they formed the basis of the civil service examinations. He held that all things arise from the union of qi, a vital or material force, and li, a rational principle, and that the source and sum of li is the taiji, the Supreme Ultimate. Qi obscures each person's perfect moral nature, so moral cultivation means clearing the qi. He advocated the investigation of things and practised a daily meditation called jingzuo.

He died on 23 April 1200. Almost a thousand people attended his funeral, although his teachings had been severely attacked. In 1208 Emperor Ningzong of Song rehabilitated him, and in 1241 a memorial tablet was placed to him in the Confucian Temple at Qufu. His teaching became influential in Japan, where it is called Shushigaku, in Korea, where it became an orthodoxy known as Jujahak, and in Vietnam.
zhuge-liang: Zhuge Liang's ancestral home was in Yangdu County, Langya Commandery, in present-day Shandong. Orphaned young, he was raised by Zhuge Xuan, a cousin of his father, whom he accompanied to Jing Province, where Zhuge Xuan lived with the governor Liu Biao. Zhuge Liang later lived in seclusion at Longzhong and earned the sobriquet Sleeping Dragon. The hermit Sima Hui and Xu Shu both recommended him to the warlord Liu Bei, who visited him three times. Zhuge Liang then proposed the Longzhong Plan: to secure Jing and Yi provinces, ally with Eastern Wu and resist Cao Wei.

In the autumn of 208 Cao Cao invaded Jing Province. Liu Bei fled to Xiakou, was defeated at the Battle of Changban, and sent Zhuge Liang to Sun Quan to propose an alliance. Sun Quan sent Zhou Yu, Cheng Pu, Lu Su and others with 30,000 troops, and in the winter of 208 the allies won a decisive victory over Cao Cao at the Battle of Red Cliffs. Defeated at the Battle of Xiaoting in 222, Liu Bei fell ill and in early 223 summoned Zhuge Liang, telling him to assist the heir but to make his own decision if the heir proved incompetent.

As regent for Liu Shan, Zhuge Liang refused letters from Wei officials urging Shu to submit. In 225 to 227 he led a southern campaign into Nanzhong against rebellions, following Ma Su's advice to win the hearts of the people. In 227 he sent Liu Shan the memorial Chu Shi Biao and gathered troops at Hanzhong. In 228 his army reached Mount Qi, and three Wei commanderies went over to Shu. In 234 he camped more than 100,000 troops on the Wuzhang Plains, where soldiers grew crops alongside civilians.

After a stalemate of more than 100 days, Zhuge Liang became critically ill and died in camp, between 11 September and 10 October 234, aged 54 by East Asian reckoning. Liu Shan gave him the posthumous title Marquis Zhongwu. As governor of Yi Province he ruled by strict law and helped write the legal codes of Shu Han. The Chu Shi Biao is regarded as a masterpiece of Chinese prose. In the 14th-century Romance of the Three Kingdoms he is a near-sage of wisdom and loyalty, and temples to the Marquis of Wu stand in Chengdu and Baidicheng.
ziaur-rahman: Ziaur Rahman was born on 19 January 1936 in the village of Bagbari in Gabtali, Bogura District. He graduated from the Pakistan Military Academy in September 1955 and was commissioned in the Pakistan Army, serving in the Punjab Regiment and from 1957 in the East Bengal Regiment. In June 1969 he was posted to Chittagong as second-in-command of the 8th East Bengal Regiment.

After the army crackdown and the arrest of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman on 26 March 1971, he revolted, and on 27 March he broadcast the declaration of independence from the Kalurghat radio station, becoming known as the Announcer of the Liberation. He commanded Sector 1 of the Bangladesh Forces, then Sector 11 from June and Z Force from mid-July.

After Mujibur Rahman was assassinated on 15 August 1975, Ziaur Rahman became Chief of Army Staff. A coup on 3 November forced him out and put him under house arrest, and on 7 November the Sipahi-Janata Revolution freed him and returned him to the post. He then held de facto power under martial law, took over the presidency on 21 April 1977 and retired from the army in 1978 as a lieutenant general.

Ziaur Rahman lifted martial law and in 1978 won a five-year term as president; elections to the National Assembly followed the next year, and opponents questioned their integrity. In 1978 he founded the Bangladesh Nationalist Party and reinstated multi-party politics and freedom of the press. He announced a 19-point programme stressing self-reliance, rural development, decentralisation, free markets and population control, set up village councils called Gram Sarkar, and launched a food-for-work programme in 1977.

He improved relations with the West and China and moved away from Mujib's close alignment with India. He also amended the constitution to open its preamble with an invocation of Allah and to replace the commitment to secularism with trust and faith in Almighty Allah. Critics say this changed the nature of the republic.

Ziaur Rahman faced many coup attempts, for which military tribunals were set up and at least 200 soldiers of the army and air force were executed. On 29 May 1981 he travelled to Chittagong to settle a dispute in the regional BNP and stayed at the Circuit House. In the early hours of 30 May a group of army officers assassinated him; six bodyguards and two aides were also killed. Nearly two million people are estimated to have attended his funeral. Opinion on his legacy is divided: he is credited with ending disorder and restoring multi-party politics, while critics say he suppressed opposition and gave posts to men accused in the killing of Mujibur Rahman.
ziggurat: The word ziggurat comes from the Akkadian ziqqurratum, from a verb meaning to protrude or to build high. Before the ziggurats there were raised platforms, which date from the Ubaid period in the sixth millennium BCE. The ziggurats began as platforms, usually oval, rectangular or square. Ziggurats mark Mesopotamian cities from about 2200 until 500 BCE. The Great Ziggurat of Ur was built by King Ur-Nammu in about the 21st century BCE, in the period of the Third Dynasty of Ur, and dedicated to Nanna, or Sîn. Sumerians, Akkadians, Kassites, Elamites, Eblaites and Babylonians all built them for local religions.

A ziggurat was a terraced structure of receding stories, each step slightly smaller than the one below. Its core was of sun-baked brick with a facing of fired brick on the outside. The facings were often glazed in different colours, which may have had astrological significance, and kings sometimes had their names engraved on the bricks. The number of levels ranged from two to seven. Each ziggurat stood in a temple complex that included a courtyard, storage rooms, bathrooms and living quarters, around which a city spread.

Designs ranged from a simple base carrying a temple, such as the White Temple of Uruk, to tall structures of many terraces. The ziggurat at Babylon, called Etemenanki, meant House of the foundation of heaven and earth in Sumerian. Chogha Zanbil in western Iran is one of the best-preserved examples.

The Mesopotamians believed the ziggurat was a dwelling place of the gods, and each city had its own patron god. It was not a place for public worship. Only priests could enter the ziggurat or the rooms at its base, and it was their duty to care for the gods and attend to their needs. The priests were very powerful members of Sumerian and Assyro-Babylonian society. Access to the top was by ramps on one side or by a spiral ramp.

The archaeologist Harriet Crawford observes that the only evidence for a shrine on top comes from Herodotus, and no physical remains of one exist, since erosion has reduced the surviving ziggurats to a fraction of their height. She suggests as a working hypothesis that small shrines stood on the highest stages. Scholars also suggest that the height offered priests refuge from the annual floods.
ziggurat-of-ur: The Sumerian name of the ziggurat was Etemenniguru, meaning house whose foundation creates terror. King Ur-Nammu of the Third Dynasty of Ur dedicated it to Nanna, the moon god and patron deity of Ur, in about the 21st century BCE on the short chronology. It was part of a temple complex that served as an administrative centre for the city. Its completion fell to King Shulgi, who proclaimed himself a god to win the allegiance of cities, and during his 48-year reign Ur became the capital of a state controlling much of Mesopotamia.

The Sumerian structure was a massive stepped pyramid measuring 64 metres in length, 45 metres in width and over 30 metres in height, though the height is speculative, since only the foundations survived. By the 6th century BCE it had crumbled to ruins. King Nabonidus, the last king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, found little left but the last stage and nothing to guide him as to its original appearance, and had it restored in seven stages rather than three.

What remains is a three-layered solid mass of mud brick faced with burnt bricks set in bitumen. The lowest layer corresponds to Ur-Nammu's construction, and the two upper layers belong to the Neo-Babylonian restoration. It is the best preserved of the ziggurats known from Mesopotamia after that of Dur Untash (Chogha Zanbil).

William Loftus rediscovered the remains in 1850, and John Taylor's excavations in the 1850s led to the identification of the site as Ur. Sir Leonard Woolley excavated it extensively between 1922 and 1934 for the University Museum of the University of Pennsylvania and the British Museum. In the 1980s the facade of the lowest level and the monumental staircase were rebuilt under Saddam Hussein. Small arms fire in the Gulf War of 1991 damaged the rebuilt ziggurat, leaving over 400 bullet holes in its walls.
zimbabwe: Zimbabwe is a landlocked country between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers, bordered by South Africa, Botswana, Zambia and Mozambique. Most of it sits on the Zimbabwean Plateau, generally over 1,000 metres high. The Eastern Highlands are mountainous, and Mount Nyangani, at 2,592 metres, is the highest point. About 20 per cent of the country is low-lying veld under 900 metres. Victoria Falls lies in the extreme north-west on the Zambezi. The climate is subtropical, the rainy season runs from late October to March, and the country faces recurring droughts.

The earliest known inhabitants were most likely the San, who left arrowheads and cave paintings, and Bantu-speaking farmers arrived approximately 2,000 years ago. Societies speaking proto-Shona languages emerged in the middle Limpopo valley in the 9th century, and the plateau became the centre of Shona states from about the 10th century. Trade with Arab merchants on the coast helped develop the Kingdom of Mapungubwe in the 13th century. By 1300 the Kingdom of Zimbabwe eclipsed it, building on its stone architecture at Great Zimbabwe, near Masvingo. These states traded gold, ivory and copper for cloth and glass.

From about 1450 to 1760 the Kingdom of Mutapa ruled much of present-day Zimbabwe and parts of central Mozambique. The British South Africa Company of Cecil Rhodes demarcated Rhodesia in 1890 and conquered Matabeleland in 1893 after the First Matabele War. Southern Rhodesia became a self-governing colony in 1923, and in 1965 the white minority government unilaterally declared independence as Rhodesia. A 15-year guerrilla war ended in a peace agreement, and Zimbabwe gained sovereignty in April 1980.

Robert Mugabe became Prime Minister in 1980 and was President from 1987 until he resigned in 2017 following a coup. The name comes from a Shona term for Great Zimbabwe, often explained as dzimba-dza-mabwe, houses of stones; the archaeologist Peter Garlake instead derives it from dzimba-hwe, venerated houses. The Shona are about 82 per cent of the population and the Ndebele 14 per cent. Zimbabwe has 16 official languages, of which English, Shona and Ndebele are most used, and its population is roughly 17.3 million.
zinder: Zinder lies 861 km east of the capital Niamey and 240 km north of the Nigerian city of Kano. Locally it is also called Damagaram. The centre consists of three main areas. In the north is Zengou, or Zango, the old Tuareg suburb, known for its vernacular architecture. In the south lies Birni, the old Hausa town, which holds the Zinder Great Mosque, Fort Tanimoune, the Sultan's Palace and a museum. Between them is Sabon Gari, the new town, which is the commercial centre and has a large market, the Grand Marché. The city has many distinctive granite rocks and a long history of water shortages.

The site was first a small Hausa village called Zengou. The town grew greatly in importance after Kanuri aristocrats arrived in 1736, built a fortified quarter named Birni to the south and made Zinder the capital of the Sultanate of Damagaram. It became an important centre of the trans-Saharan trade, with routes south through Kano and east to Bornu. The sultanate stayed nominally subject to the Borno Empire until the mid-to-late 19th century, when Sultan Tanimoune Dan Souleymane declared independence and began a period of vigorous expansion.

Europeans reached the region in the 19th century, beginning with the German explorer Heinrich Barth, who stayed in Zinder in 1851. The French explorer Marius Gabriel Cazemajou was killed in the city in 1897. After a brief resistance Zinder was occupied in July 1899 by Lt. Pallier of the Voulet-Chanoine mission. The French barracks was called Fort Cazemajou, and it served as the capital of the Niger Military Territory when that was created in 1911. In 1926 the capital was moved back to the village of Niamey, after fears of Hausa revolts and as relations improved with the Djerma of the west. After Niger became independent the fort was renamed for Sultan Tanimoune.

The city's economy rests largely on the agriculture of its surroundings. It is divided into five urban municipalities, Zinder I to Zinder V, and has an airport a few kilometres to the southwest and the André-Salifou University, founded in 2010. The oil refinery SORAZ, commissioned in November 2011, stands 50 km to the north and was the country's first.
zionism: The word Zion derives from Mount Zion, a hill in Jerusalem named in the Hebrew Bible, and has been used poetically for the Land of Israel since the Babylonian Exile. Religious tradition held that a future messianic age would bring a return to Zion, recalled in the phrase next year in Jerusalem, and that the return should come through Divine Providence rather than human action. Forerunners of Zionism were thinkers and activists such as the rabbis Judah Alkalai and Zvi Hirsch Kalischer, whose Seeking Zion of 1862 was the first written work to demand mass migration of Jews to Palestine.

Modern Zionism emerged in Central and Eastern Europe as a secular nationalist movement in the late 19th century, in reaction to new waves of antisemitism and in response to the Haskalah, or Jewish Enlightenment. By the early 20th century the movement, led by Theodor Herzl, tied this national revival to Palestine, then under Ottoman rule.

Fundamental to Zionism is the belief that Jews constitute a nation with a right and need of self-determination. Early Zionism was ambiguous about the form this would take: the Basel declaration spoke of a Jewish homeland and the Balfour Declaration of 1917 of a national home, and according to Shlomo Avineri a sovereign state became the fully articulated goal only in the 1930s.

Zionist views have not been uniform. The mainstream has included Liberal, Labor, Revisionist and Cultural Zionism. Revisionist Zionism, developed by Ze'ev Jabotinsky, who founded the Revisionist Party in 1925, sought a state on both sides of the Jordan and held that Arab resistance would have to be met with an iron wall of military force. Cultural Zionism, founded by Ahad Ha'am, looked to Palestine as a spiritual and cultural centre, and Religious Zionism, associated with Abraham Isaac Kook, combines religious conservatism with nationalism.

Britain's 1917 Balfour Declaration supported a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, and the 1922 Mandate placed Britain in control until 1948, when the State of Israel declared its independence and war broke out. Advocates view Zionism as a national liberation movement for the return of an indigenous people to the homeland of its ancestors. Opponents often describe it as a colonialist or racist ideology; scholars such as Edward Said and Joseph Massad place it within European colonialism, while Anita Shapira and Shlomo Ben-Ami frame it as a liberation movement that used colonial methods. Before the Second World War many Jews also opposed it, among them Orthodox Jews, who held that it pre-empted the Messiah.
zittau: Zittau lies in Upper Lusatia, the southern part of Lusatia, on the Mandau and the Lusatian Neisse, in the Zittau Basin just north of the Zittau Mountains, which are part of the Sudetes. The Lusatian Neisse forms the border with Poland and touches the city in the east, and the two rivers meet in its south-east. Further south is the point where Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic meet. The city belongs to the district of Görlitz and has about 25,000 inhabitants.

The city grew from a Slavic settlement of the 12th century. The area belonged to the Bohemian duchy, later kingdom, from the 11th century. It was first mentioned as Sitavia in 1238 and received town rights in 1255 from King Ottokar II of Bohemia, who also built defensive walls. In 1319 it passed to the Piast-ruled Duchy of Jawor, and after the death of Duke Henry I of Jawor in 1346 it returned to the Bohemian Crown. Its coat of arms still shows a Czech lion and a Silesian Piast eagle. In 1469 it recognized the Hungarian king Matthias Corvinus as ruler, and after his death in 1490 it returned to Bohemia, then under Vladislaus II. In 1635 it passed to the Electorate of Saxony.

In 1346 Zittau became a member of the Six-City League of Upper Lusatia, and it was given the title Die Reiche, the Rich, because of its high proportion of well-to-do citizens. Great fires struck it in 1359 and 1422. Beer was one of its most important trading goods in the 16th century, and textiles became important in the 18th and 19th centuries, as elsewhere in Upper Lusatia. After the Battle of White Mountain in 1620, many Protestant refugees from Bohemia were taken in by the Protestant Saxon rulers at Zittau. The near-complete destruction of the city in the Seven Years' War means that its earlier prosperity survives in only a few exceptional buildings and in the cemeteries where the well-to-do were buried.

The Great Zittau Lenten Cloth of 1472, a veil of 56 square metres that hid the altar during Lent, is shown in the former Church of the Holy Cross, and a smaller Lenten cloth of 1573 is kept in the Museum of Cultural History in the former Franciscan monastery. The city hall, designed by Karl Friedrich Schinkel in the style of an Italian palazzo, was built between 1840 and 1845, and the Church of Our Lady is first mentioned in 1355. Several historic fountains stand in the squares, among them the Roland or Mars Fountain of 1585. The composer Heinrich Marschner was born in Zittau in 1795.
ziusudra: One version of the Sumerian King List, the recension known as WB-62 or the Weld-Blundell prism, names Ziusudra of Shuruppak as the last king of Sumer before the flood. It makes him the son of Ubara-Tutu, from whom he inherited the rule, and says that he reigned as both king and gudug priest for ten sars, periods of 3,600 years, a figure that is probably a copyist's error for ten years.

Sediment layers at Shuruppak, the modern Tell Fara, and at Uruk, Kish and other sites attest a river flood radiocarbon-dated to about 2900 BCE, and Kish flourished soon after it. On this ground Max Mallowan held that there were good reasons to believe Ziusudra was a prehistoric ruler of a historic city.

The Sumerian tale survives on a single fragmentary tablet, dated by its script to the 17th century BCE and published in 1914 by Arno Poebel. Its first part tells of the creation of humans and animals and the founding of the first cities, Eridu, Bad-tibira, Larak, Sippar and Shuruppak. The passages in which the gods decide on the flood and in which the boat is described are lost. Where the text resumes, a storm rages for seven days. The sun god Utu then appears, and Ziusudra opens a window, prostrates himself and sacrifices an ox and a sheep.

After another gap he bows before the gods An and Enlil, who give him breath eternal. The rest of the poem is lost. The word used for his new home in Dilmun, kur, is ambiguous. Samuel Noah Kramer explained that its first meaning is mountain, from which came the senses of foreign land and of land in general.

Ziusudra is one of several heroes of Near Eastern flood stories, with Atrahasis, Utnapishtim and the biblical Noah, and many elements are shared among the versions. The eleventh tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh calls Utnapishtim man of Shuruppak. Ziusudra is also named in The Death of Gilgamesh, The Poem of Early Rulers and a late version of the Instructions of Shuruppak, a text Kramer dated to about 2600 BCE.

In Greek he became Xisuthros, known from the writings of Berossus, a priest of Bel in Babylon. In that version the god Enki is identified with the Greek Cronus, Xisuthros is the son of one Ardates and reigns 18 saroi, reckoned as 64,800 years, and his reed boat is said to have survived until Berossus's own day in the Corcyrean Mountains of Armenia.
zlin: The first written mention of Zlín is from 1322, when it was acquired by Queen Elizabeth Richeza. It was already a market town and a craft guild centre for the surrounding region of Moravian Wallachia. From 1358 the estate belonged to Bishop Albrecht of Šternberk and became the seat of the Moravian branch of the Šternberk family, and in 1397 its town privileges were extended. The Hussite Wars forced the family to sell it in 1437. The 16th century brought peace and prosperity, with drapery, pottery and shoemaking flourishing.

Tomáš Baťa and his siblings founded a shoe factory in 1894. By 1922 it was the leading maker of footwear in Czechoslovakia, and the company moved into engineering, chemistry and rubber technology. Baťa was elected mayor in 1923. Between 1923 and 1938 the company built a large complex on the outskirts with thousands of flats, schools, department stores, scientific facilities and a hospital, in a controlled development shaped by modern urban ideas. The plan was the work of František Lydie Gahura, who had studied in Le Corbusier's atelier, and the city drew on both Ebenezer Howard's garden city and Le Corbusier's vision of urban modernity.

Buildings of the period include Baťa's Hospital of 1927, the Grand Cinema of 1932, with 2,270 seats the largest cinema in Central Europe in its time, and the Tomas Bata Memorial of 1933. Baťa's Skyscraper, built in 1936–1939 to a design by Vladimír Karfík, rose 77.5 m.

Tomáš Baťa died in 1932 and the company was run by others. German occupation halted development in the Second World War, and in 1944 American bombing destroyed large parts of the factories. Soviet and Romanian armies liberated the city on 2 May 1945, and in October 1945 the Bata company in Czechoslovakia was nationalised. The city name returned to Zlín on 1 January 1990. Zlín has about 75,000 inhabitants, lies on the Dřevnice River about 70 km east of Brno, is the seat of the Zlín Region and has been home to Tomas Bata University since 2001. Much of its centre is protected as an urban monument zone.
znojmo: Znojmo lies in the South Moravian Region, about 54 kilometres south-west of Brno and near the border with Austria. It stands mainly on a rock outcrop on the steep left bank of the Thaya, along the eastern edge of Podyjí National Park. The name is of uncertain origin. The likeliest explanations derive it either from the Old Czech words znoj, heat, and znojný, exposed to heat, or from a personal name, Znojem or Znojim.

A settlement may have existed in the time of Great Moravia in the 9th century, when the main gord stood on the hill across the Gránický brook and was one of the first places in Moravia where Christianity appeared. After 1029 the gord was the residence of a Přemyslid principality within the Bohemian March of Moravia and a strategic outpost near the Bavarian March of Austria. Around 1100 the administrative centre moved to a new castle, and in 1101 Duke Luitpold of Znojmo built the Rotunda of Saint Catherine there. Duke Vladislaus II of Bohemia seized and demolished the castle in 1145, and in 1190 Duke Conrad II founded the Premonstratensian Louka Monastery.

King Ottokar I of Bohemia founded the royal town shortly before 1226, in front of the rebuilt castle, and fortified it; it was one of the first royal towns in Moravia. Znojmo survived the Hussite Wars unscathed, as the Hussites failed to capture it. In the 15th and 16th centuries burgher houses with a system of underground passages were built as part of the fortifications. The population was mixed Czech and German, and the burghers mainly spoke German. The Thirty Years' War ended the town's development, and it took over a hundred years to recover. The Armistice of Znaim was concluded there on 12 July 1809, after the Battle of Wagram.

Znojmo has about 34,000 inhabitants and is the second most populated town of its region. Its well-preserved historic centre is protected as an urban monument reservation, and the Rotunda of Saint Catherine, the Louka Monastery and the Town Hall Tower, built in 1445-1448, are national cultural monuments. The town is known for its gherkins, grown in the region since 1571 when George II, abbot of Louka, introduced them, and for winemaking.
zoe-porphyrogenita: Zoe was called Porphyrogenita, born into the purple, the name given to a child born in the capital to a reigning emperor. She was the second daughter of Constantine VIII and his wife Helena. Her uncle Basil II, the senior emperor, prevented his nieces from marrying into the Byzantine nobility, since a husband would have gained a claim on the throne, and Zoe lived in obscurity in the women's quarters of the palace for many years. A marriage to the Holy Roman Emperor Otto III was planned in 996. In 1001 an embassy under Arnulf II, Archbishop of Milan, chose Zoe, then 23, from the emperor's three daughters, and she sailed for Italy in January 1002, only to learn at Bari that Otto had died.

Constantine became sole emperor in December 1025. Hoping to continue the dynasty, he sought an aristocratic husband for one of his daughters. Constantine Dalassenos was rejected, and Romanos Argyros, the urban prefect of Constantinople, was chosen after her sister Theodora refused him. Zoe and Romanos married on 10 November 1028, and the next day Constantine died and they took the throne.

Zoe was desperate to bear a child and used charms and potions without effect. Romanos grew distant, and in 1033 she took up with a low-born servant named Michael. Romanos was found dying in his bath on 11 April 1034. Michael Psellus says some of his retinue held his head under the water; John Scylitzes says he was drowned on Michael's orders; Matthew of Edessa has Zoe poisoning him. Zoe and Michael married that day, and Michael IV was crowned the next. He excluded her from politics, and his brother John the Orphanotrophos governed in his name.

In 1041 John forced Zoe to adopt his nephew Michael Kalaphates, who became Michael V when Michael IV died on 10 December. He banished her to a monastery on Principus, which provoked a popular uprising. On 19 April 1042 the mob rose for Zoe and Theodora, and they were crowned on 21 April as joint empresses. After two months Zoe married Constantine Monomachos on 11 June 1042, and he was crowned Constantine IX. She remained Augusta.

Constantine IX brought his mistress Maria Skleraina to court and gave her the title of sebaste. Rumours that she planned to murder Zoe led to a popular uprising in 1044, quieted when Zoe and Theodora appeared on a balcony. Psellos describes Zoe in later life as deeply pious, consulting a jewelled statue of Christ for omens, and also as extravagant and vindictive. She died in 1050, aged 72, and was buried in Constantinople. Constantine tried to have her canonised, but the attempt foundered on her history of affairs.
zog-i: Zog was born Ahmed Muhtar Bey Zogolli in 1895 at Burgajet Castle, near Burrel in northern Albania. His landowning family was of beylical rank, with feudal authority over the region of Mati, and his mother belonged to the Toptani family, who claimed descent from the sister of Skanderbeg. He was educated at the Galatasaray High School in Istanbul and became governor of Mat when his father died in 1911. In 1912 he took part in the Albanian Declaration of Independence. In the First World War he volunteered on the side of Austria-Hungary and was detained in Vienna and Rome before returning to Albania in 1919.

In the early 1920s he served as Governor of Shkodër, Minister of the Interior and chief of the military, and in 1922 changed his surname to Zogu, which sounds more Albanian. He became prime minister that year at 27, and in February 1924 he was shot and wounded in Parliament. A leftist revolt drove him into exile in June 1924, and he came back with Yugoslav and White Russian military backing.

The Constituent Assembly elected Zogu the first President of Albania on 21 January 1925. A new constitution gave him sweeping executive and legislative powers, so that he was in effect a dictator. His government enacted major reforms, and its principal ally was Italy, which lent money in exchange for a greater role in Albanian finances. It was also a police state in which civil liberties were almost non-existent, the press was censored and opponents were imprisoned and often killed. In 1925 he ceded Sveti Naum to Yugoslavia.

On 1 September 1928 Albania became a kingdom and Zogu proclaimed himself Zog I, King of the Albanians. He was never formally crowned. In 1929 he abolished Islamic law and adopted a civil code based on the Swiss one. In 1938 he opened Albania's borders to Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi Germany, and he married Countess Geraldine Apponyi in April of that year. Their son Leka was born on 5 April 1939. Zog reputedly survived more than 55 assassination attempts.

Through the 1930s Albania became almost wholly dependent on Mussolini's Italy. Italy invaded in April 1939, and Zog went into exile, never to return. He lived in England during the Second World War. The new Communist-dominated government under Enver Hoxha barred his return and formally dethroned him in 1946. He spent the rest of his life in France and died on 9 April 1961. His remains were moved from the Thiais Cemetery near Paris to a royal mausoleum in Tirana in 2012.
zollverein: By the 1790s the Holy Roman Empire had about 1,800 customs barriers, and in the early 19th century Prussia itself had more than 67 local tariffs. A shipment from Königsberg to Cologne was inspected and taxed about 80 times. The Congress of Vienna created the German Confederation in 1815 but made no effort at trade standardisation. In 1818 Prussia abolished its own internal tariffs, and it then began inviting other states to do the same. Historians have identified three Prussian aims: to eliminate Austrian influence in Germany, to improve the economies, and to strengthen Germany against French aggression while reducing the economic independence of the smaller states.

The middle-sized states had their own plans. In 1825 an agreement at Stuttgart between Württemberg and Bavaria founded the South German Customs Union, and Hanover, Saxony, Hesse and others made trade agreements of their own. Organised by the treaties of 1833, the Zollverein formally started on 1 January 1834, and that year Baden and Württemberg joined the Prussian union, which was renamed the German Customs Union. By 1835 it included most of the states of the German Confederation. Austria stayed out because of its highly protectionist trade policy and Prince von Metternich's opposition.

The union was not ended by the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 but was reorganised in 1867, when no individual state any longer had a veto. By then its members covered about 425,000 square kilometres. After the founding of the German Empire in 1871 the Empire took over control of the union, though Hamburg acceded only in 1888, with part of its port left outside. Luxembourg remained a member until 1919, when the Treaty of Versailles ended its membership.

It was the first instance in history in which independent states formed a full economic union without a political federation. Economic historians Helmut Böhme and H.-U. Wehler hold that it laid the groundwork for unification under Prussian guidance. Hans-Joachim Voth and others dispute this, arguing that smaller states joined for fiscal reasons and used the revenue to consolidate their independence, and that membership brought no political commitment to Berlin in 1866. In 1840 the poet August Heinrich Hoffmann von Fallersleben published an ironic song, Der deutsche Zollverein.
zoltan-kodaly: Kodály was born in Kecskemét, in the Kingdom of Hungary within Austria-Hungary, on 16 December 1882, and learned the violin as a child. In 1900 he entered the Department of Languages at the University of Budapest and at the same time Hans von Kössler's composition class at the Royal Hungarian Academy of Music. After his studies he spent a year in Paris with Charles-Marie Widor.

In 1905 he visited remote villages to collect songs on phonograph cylinders, and in 1906 he wrote a thesis on Hungarian folk song, Strophic Construction in Hungarian Folksong. About then he met Béla Bartók, whom he took under his wing and introduced to some of the methods of folk-song collecting. The two became lifelong friends and champions of each other's music.

In 1919 Kodály was appointed alongside Bartók to the Music Directory by the People's Commissariat for Education and Culture in the short-lived Hungarian Soviet Republic. His works blend western European styles, including classical, late-romantic, impressionist and modernist traditions, with the folk music of Hungary and of the Hungarian-inhabited areas of what are now Slovakia and Romania.

Partly because of the Great War and the geopolitical changes that followed, and partly because of a diffident temperament in youth, he had no major public success until 1923. In that year Psalmus Hungaricus was first performed at a concert for the fiftieth anniversary of the union of Buda and Pest, at which Bartók's Dance Suite also had its premiere.

His later works include the stage work Háry János (1926) and its suite, the Dances of Marosszék (1929), the Dances of Galánta (1933), the Variations on a Hungarian folk song, The Peacock (1939), the Concerto for Orchestra (1940) and the Symphony in memoriam Toscanini (1961).

Beginning in 1935 Kodály worked with his colleague Jenő Ádám on a project to reform music teaching in Hungarian schools. He wrote down no comprehensive method but set out principles: music is for everyone, teaching should be sequential and begin with the child, singing is the first and most valuable tool, and teachers should draw on quality folk songs in the pupils' mother tongue. These principles were widely taken up after World War II, above all in Hungary but also in many other countries. Kodály died in Budapest on 6 March 1967, at the age of 84. The city of Pécs commissioned a bronze statue of him by Imre Varga in 1976.
zoroastrianism: The roots of Zoroastrianism lie in a common prehistoric Indo-Iranian religious system dating back to the early 2nd millennium BCE, and the religion shares many elements with Vedic religion. Zoroaster, whom tradition places in the 6th century BCE, is thought by many modern historians to have lived much earlier, in the second half of the second millennium BCE; the date is uncertain. He was born into the Spitama clan and calls himself a poet-priest and prophet in the Gathas. The religion enters recorded history in the mid-5th century BCE, when Herodotus describes Iranian customs that may be recognizably Zoroastrian, among them exposure of the dead.

Zoroastrians exalt Ahura Mazda, the uncreated, all-wise creator, and hold the Gathas, hymns thought to be Zoroaster's own, to be the most sacred texts. In the Gathas the central dualism is ethical, a choice between Asha, truth and order, and Druj, the lie. Evil is embodied in Angra Mainyu, the destructive spirit, and Ahura Mazda is served by the Amesha Spentas and by divine beings called Yazatas. Scholars disagree whether the faith is monotheistic, polytheistic, henotheistic or a mixture. At death each soul crosses the Chinvat Bridge, judged by the Yazatas Mithra, Sraosha and Rashnu. The Avesta is the central collection of texts, and today worship centres on fire temples.

For about a thousand years Zoroastrianism was the official religion of successive Iranian polities, from the Achaemenid Empire, which formalised many of its rituals, to the Sasanian Empire, which revived the faith and standardised its teachings. Over 22 years in the 7th century the Muslim caliphate conquered most of the Sasanian Empire, and the faith began to decline. Persecution by the early Muslims prompted many to migrate to India, where they became the Parsis. Zoroastrians now live mainly in India, Iran and diaspora communities, and India's census of 2011 recorded 57,264 Parsis. Some credit the faith with an imprint on Second Temple Judaism and, through it, on later monotheistic religions.
zubarah: Zubarah lies on the north-western coast of the Qatar peninsula in the Al Shamal municipality, about 105 km from Doha. The site covers around 400 hectares, 60 of them inside the outer town wall, and is Qatar's most substantial archaeological site. It stands on a low coastal hillock between sabkha flats and stony desert. Fresh water was scarce, so Murair Fort was built 1.8 km to the east, on the edge of the desert scarp, to protect wells that tapped shallow freshwater lenses. The name is most often linked to an Arabic word for a raised sand mound.

The Bani Utbah clans, among them the Al Sabah, Al Khalifa and Al Jalahma, migrated from the Najd in response to drought, travelling through Al Aflaj, Qatif and Al Ahsa to Freiha in north-western Qatar. In the 1760s the growing influence of the Al Khalifa brought conflict with the Al Musallam clan, which acted for the Bani Khalid. Sheikh Muhammad bin Khalifa refused its demand for tribute, and a fortified settlement, Qal'at Murair, was finished by 1768. The town was attacked at the behest of Nasr Al-Madhkur in 1778 and 1782.

Zubarah lived by pearling and trade. Its boats sailed to pearl beds along the southern shore of the Gulf for weeks at a time, and the pearl trade employed up to a third of the male population of the region until cultured pearls appeared in the early 1900s. The population at its height is estimated at 6,000 to 9,000. The Wahhabis occupied the town in 1809. In 1811 Said bin Sultan of Muscat attacked their garrisons and the fort was burned. Most remaining residents left in the early 20th century because the water supply was inadequate.

The town was laid out on a grid of streets, with courtyard houses of local stone coated in gypsum plaster, a market with storage rooms and a wall 2.5 km long defended by 22 semi-circular towers. Excavation found 27 date presses. Danish expeditions first surveyed the site in 1956, and the Qatar Museums Authority excavated in the 1980s and from 2002 to 2003. Since 2009 Copenhagen University has worked there with the Qatar Islamic Archaeology and Heritage Project. The Al Zubara Fort, built in 1938, also stands there.
zugdidi: Zugdidi lies in the north-west of the historical province of Samegrelo, also called Mingrelia, 318 kilometres west of Tbilisi. It stands at an elevation of 100 to 110 metres, about 30 kilometres from the Black Sea coast and 30 kilometres from the Egrisi Range. The name first appeared in the 17th century and means big hill in the Mingrelian language, after a hill in the eastern part of the city where small remains of an ancient fortress can still be seen. The city is the seat of the Metropolitan of Zugdidi and Tsaishi of the Georgian Orthodox Church.

Zugdidi was the capital of the Principality of Mingrelia, also called Odishi, until the Russian Empire abolished the principality in 1867. It then became the administrative centre of the Zugdidi Uyezd in the Kutais Governorate until 1918, when it passed to the Democratic Republic of Georgia. Between the 17th and 19th centuries it was an important political and cultural centre of Mingrelia and of Georgia as a whole. In 1646 the medieval epic The Knight in the Panther's Skin was rewritten there by Mamuka Tavakalashvili at the court of Prince Levan II Dadiani.

During the Crimean War Ottoman forces under Omar Pasha seized the town in 1855, and at the end of 1855 and the beginning of 1856 it was liberated by the Mingrelian Militia under Major General Prince Grigol Dadiani. On the order of Iskender Pasha the Ottomans plundered, burned and destroyed the whole city, especially the palaces and the botanical garden, and its population fell from 2,000 to 800. From 1930 it was the centre of the Zugdidi Raion of the Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic. Many buildings were heavily damaged in the Georgian Civil War of 1992–1993, and refugees from Abkhazia moved to the city.

The Dadiani Palace, built in the 19th century, was home to the last ruling family of the Principality of Samegrelo. The complex includes the palace of Ekaterine Dadiani, a residence for her son Niko Dadiani, a monastery and the botanical garden. The palace is now a museum.

The Shalva Dadiani Drama Theatre staged its first performance, Molière's Le médecin malgré lui, on 11 April 1869, and the first public library opened in 1887, though the library tradition goes back to Prince David Dadiani, who ruled from 1812 to 1853 and collected many books. Zugdidi is the regional centre of Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti.
zuiderzee: The Zuiderzee was a shallow bay of the North Sea in the northwest of the Netherlands. It extended about 100 km inland and at most 50 km in width, with a depth of about 4 to 5 m, a coastline of about 300 km and an area of 5,000 square kilometres. Its name is Dutch for southern sea, which shows that it originates in Friesland, to the north. Five small islands lay within it, Wieringen, Urk, Schokland, Pampus and Marken, whose people lived mainly by fishing. Around it fishing villages grew up and several became walled towns with extensive trade, in particular Kampen, and later Amsterdam, Hoorn and Enkhuizen.

In classical times the water here was called Lake Flevo by Roman authors, the largest of a region of lowland and freshwater lakes, separated from the sea by a belt of marsh and fen and fed by streams including the Vecht, Eem and IJssel. It drained to the North Sea through the Vlie. The Roman geographer Pomponius Mela describes it in 44 CE. In the early Middle Ages it was called Almere, a name in a life of saints by the Anglo-Saxon Boniface in 753, perhaps meaning eel lake.

Rising sea levels, peat digging by the Frisians and floods turned the lake into an inland sea. The All Saints' Flood of 1170 broke through the barrier dunes near Texel and washed away land between Stavoren, Texel and Medemblik, and its disaster marked the rise of Amsterdam, since traders from the Hanseatic cities could now reach the area. Further surges in 1173 and 1196 and in the 13th century completed the change, and about 1400 the Zuiderzee had reached its full extent. Storms pushing North Sea water into the inlet often caused floods and lost ships. On 18 November 1421 a seawall broke and flooded 72 villages and killed about 10,000 people, in the Second St Elizabeth's Flood.

Closing the Zuiderzee was first proposed in 1667, though a feasible method did not appear until the 20th century. The Flood of January 1916 hastened plans originating from Cornelius Lely, and the Afsluitdijk was built between 1927 and 1932.

With the completion of the Afsluitdijk in 1932 the Zuiderzee became the freshwater IJsselmeer, and the outer part became part of the Wadden Sea. Large areas were reclaimed by polders: the Wieringermeer Polder in 1930, the Northeast Polder in 1942, Eastern Flevoland in 1957 and Southern Flevoland in 1968. Together they form the Zuiderzee Works, and the reclaimed land became the province of Flevoland. The Markerwaard, begun in 1963, was abandoned in the mid-1980s.
zulfikar-ali-bhutto: Zulfikar Ali Bhutto was born on 5 January 1928 near Larkana in Sindh, the third child of Shah Nawaz Bhutto, dewan of the princely state of Junagadh, and Khursheed Begum. He studied at the University of Southern California, the University of California, Berkeley and the University of Oxford, and trained as a barrister at Lincoln's Inn. In 1958 he became Pakistan's youngest cabinet minister, in charge of Commerce under President Iskander Mirza.

He then served President Ayub Khan and became foreign minister in 1963, drawing Pakistan close to China. After the 1965 war with India and the Tashkent Declaration he was dismissed. On 30 November 1967 he and others founded the Pakistan Peoples Party in Lahore, whose creed he summed up as Islam as faith, democracy as policy and socialism as economy.

In the general election of 7 December 1970 the Awami League won a majority in the legislature, while Bhutto's party was the largest in West Pakistan. Bhutto refused to accept an Awami League government. Talks failed, the army began Operation Searchlight on 25 March 1971, and civil war and a war with India led to the creation of Bangladesh. On 20 December 1971 Bhutto took over from Yahya Khan as president and as the first civilian Chief Martial Law Administrator.

He secured the release of 93,000 prisoners of war and, through the Simla Agreement of July 1972, the return of five thousand square miles of territory. A constitution drafted with the opposition was approved in 1973 by 97 percent of parliament, and on 14 August 1973 he was sworn in as prime minister. He nationalised industry and brought in Abdul Qadeer Khan to begin a nuclear programme. In Balochistan he dismissed the provincial government in 1973 and ordered a military operation.

After the 1977 elections the opposition Pakistan National Alliance alleged vote rigging and unrest spread. On 5 July 1977 General Zia-ul-Haq seized power and detained Bhutto. He was arrested again on 3 September, charged with authorising the murder of Nawab Muhammad Ahmed Khan Kasuri in March 1974, sentenced to death on 18 March 1978, and executed on 4 April 1979.

His legacy remains disputed. Supporters call him Quaid-e-Awām, the People's Leader, and praise his nationalism and the 1973 constitution. Critics point to the economic setbacks they blame on nationalisation and to the suppression of opponents and abuses in Balochistan. His daughter Benazir Bhutto served twice as prime minister.
zulfiqar-khan: Zulfiqar Khan was born Muhammad Ismail, in 1649 according to the historian Satish Chandra or in 1657 according to William Irvine. His father, Asad Khan, became the long-serving wazir of Emperor Aurangzeb, and his mother, Mehrunissa Begum, was a daughter of Asaf Khan, wazir under Shah Jahan. The family was Iranian on the father's side: his grandfather had moved to India after his great-grandfather, the governor of Safavid Shirvan, was executed around 1600 by Shah Abbas I. In 1677 he married a daughter of the noble Shaista Khan and received the title Itiqad Khan.

In 1689 he captured the Maratha fort of Raigad. The Maratha king Rajaram Bhonsle escaped to Jinji, but the family of his predecessor Sambhaji, including the young Shahu, was taken, and Muhammad Ismail was given the title Zulfiqar Khan. Assigned in 1690 to the Siege of Jinji, he made slow progress against a strong fort and disrupted supply lines, and the length of the siege led contemporaries to accuse him of collusion with the enemy. In 1693 he and his father arrested Prince Kam Bakhsh for negotiating with Rajaram against orders. He became mir bakhshi, or paymaster general, in 1702.

In the war of succession of 1707 he reluctantly sided with Prince Azam Shah but deserted him at the Battle of Jajau. The victor, Bahadur Shah I, reconciled him, confirmed him as mir bakhshi and in 1709 made him governor of the Deccan. When Bahadur Shah lay dying in 1712, Zulfiqar Khan allied three of his sons against the strongest, Azim-us-Shan, and then helped Jahandar Shah, the weakest, to kill the others. For this the historian Munis Faruqui calls him the first kingmaker in Mughal history. As wazir he held effective power, abolished the jizya and continued to conciliate the Marathas.
